passages.title: The wise Book and its human messenger
passages.tafsir:
**The passage in one breath.** Sūrah Yūnus opens by placing side by side the two things the disbelievers could not reconcile: a Book rich in wisdom, and an ordinary human being carrying it. Ayah 1 names the Book; ayah 2 answers the objection to the man. One question holds the two together — how does Allah's guidance actually reach human beings? — and it is answered from both ends: the revelation is wise, and the one who delivers it is one of you.

## Where this sūrah stands

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Sūrah Yūnus is among the Makkī sūrahs; three of its verses revealed after the Hijrah to Madīnah have been called Madanī. Its business is to establish the basic objectives of the Qur'an and of Islam — the Oneness of Allah, the mission of His Messenger, and the inevitability of the Hereafter. It argues for them against the backdrop of the universe we already experience and observe, which is what makes the sūrah so easy to take in. Alongside the arguments come lesson-bearing historical accounts, placed there to warn people who do not pay heed to Allah's open signs, and, as a natural corollary, a refutation of shirk — of heedless people ascribing partners to the pristine divinity of Allah — together with answers to the doubts that cluster around it.

Reading these two ayat immediately after Sūrah At-Tawbah brings out something important about method. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that At-Tawbah pursued these same objectives by material means: it broke through the powerful cordon of kufr and shirk by waging jihād against deniers and disbelievers. The present sūrah was revealed in Makkah, before the injunctions of jihād came down at all. So here the very same objectives are established purely by arguments and evidences — very much in accordance with the law of the Makkan period. That is why ayah 2 does not answer the objectors with force but with a question that turns their astonishment back on them.

## Alif, Lām, Rā — and the discipline of not digging

The sūrah opens with the "isolated letters," الٓر. Many sūrahs of the Qur'an begin this way. Ibn Kathir simply refers the reader back to his discussion at the opening of Sūrat Al-Baqarah rather than reopening the question here.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more explicit about the attitude a believer should take. The debates of commentators over combinations like الم, حم and عسق are long. But we also have the authentic verdict of the Ṣaḥābah (the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ), the Tābiʿīn (the generation who learned directly from those Companions) and the righteous elders of this community — the *salaf* (the earliest generations) — about these letters: they are secret symbols or signs. In all likelihood the Prophet ﷺ was confided with their meaning, but he chose to disclose to his community only those areas of knowledge and insight which their minds could bear, and which, if left unknown, would have impeded the normal living of his people. Nothing a Muslim must do depends on knowing the secret of these letters, and nothing is missed by not knowing it. So the Prophet ﷺ did not tell his community about their meaning, as it was unnecessary for them.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the conclusion for us with real warmth: we too should not go about digging into it — because it is certain that had knowing their meaning been expedient for us, our master, who was mercy personified for the whole world, would never have hesitated in telling us about it.

There is a spiritual training in that. The very first thing this sūrah does is set a boundary around your curiosity: some of what Allah has revealed is for you to recite and believe, not to decode. Accepting that is itself an act of submission.

## "These are the verses of the Book, rich in wisdom"

In ayah 1, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the word تِلْكَ (*tilka*, "these") points forward — to the āyāt of this sūrah that are about to follow. "The Book" is the Qur'an. And to describe it, the Qur'an here chooses the word الْحَكِيم (*al-ḥakīm*): the Book of Wisdom.

Ibn Kathir puts the emphasis slightly differently, and it is worth holding both: this indicates that these are verses of the Qur'an *in which the wisdom of judgment is clear*. So the description is not decorative praise. It is a claim being staked before any argument has begun — that what is coming is a Book whose judgment carries visible wisdom, wisdom you can inspect.

## The objection: astonished that a man was chosen

Ayah 2 opens with a question that is really a rebuke: *"Is it astonishing to people that We have sent revelation to a man from among themselves…?"* Ibn Kathir reads it exactly that way — Allah rebukes the attitude of the disbelievers with these words.

Ibn Kathir preserves the moment behind it. Ad-Daḥḥāk reported Ibn ʿAbbās that he said: "When Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ as a Messenger, most of the Arabs denied him and his message and said: Allah is greater than sending a human Messenger like Muhammad." Ibn ʿAbbās said: "So Allah revealed: *Is it a wonder for mankind…*"

Notice the shape of the objection. It was voiced in the language of reverence — *Allah is greater than that* — and it accompanied a flat denial of the Messenger and his message. Ibn Kathir shows that this is an old habit, not a Qurayshī invention: people have always found it strange that Allah would send Messengers to them from among mankind. Earlier nations said, "Shall mere men guide us?" (64:6). Hūd and Ṣāliḥ each said to their people, "Do you wonder that there has come to you a reminder from your Lord through a man from among you?" (7:63). And the disbelievers of Quraysh said, "Has he made the gods (all) into one? Verily, this is a curious thing!" (38:5). The same objection surfaces in generation after generation.

**Why a human messenger is the only sensible arrangement.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that the mushrikūn had decided, out of their ignorance, that a messenger who comes from Allah should not be a human being (*al-bashar*) but an angel. The Qur'an has refuted this idea on several occasions from different angles. One of them: *"Say, Had there been angels walking in peace on the Earth, We would have certainly sent to them from the heavens an angel-messenger"* (17:95). The principle underneath is homogeneity — a messenger's mission cannot be accomplished unless there is a mutual likeness of kind between him and those he is sent to. Angels are homogeneous with angels; human beings with human beings. If the purpose is to send a messenger for human beings, only a human being has to be made the messenger.

The present ayah makes the same point by a different route. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān paraphrases its logic as a series of questions: why should people wonder that a human being was made a messenger? Why should it surprise them that a human being was entrusted with warning the disobedient against the punishment of Allah, and with heralding the good news of His rewards to the obedient? This kind of wondering, it says, deserves a counter-wonder — because sending a human messenger to the human race is perfect commonsense. The astonishment is not in the arrangement; it is in the people astonished by it.

## The two halves of the mission: warn, and give glad tidings

The revelation sent to that man carried a twofold commission, and the ayah states both: *"Warn mankind, and give good news to those who believe."*

Warning is addressed to *mankind* at large — in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrasing, warning the disobedient ones against the punishment of Allah. Glad tidings are addressed specifically to *those who believe* — heralding the good news of His rewards to the obedient ones. Fear and hope are not two rival temperaments in this religion; they are the two hands of one message. Ibn Kathir echoes the same pairing when he sums up what Allah had done for these people: He sent them a Messenger from among themselves, a man of their own race, "as a bearer of good news and as a warner."

## قَدَمَ صِدْقٍ — "a perfect place with their Lord"

The good news itself is expressed in an unusual phrase: *qadama ṣidqin ʿinda rabbihim*. Ibn Kathir renders the sense as "the rewards of their good deeds"; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it "a perfect place with their Lord." It repays slowing down.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens the word up. The initial meaning of قَدَم (*qadam*) here is "step," as in English. Since a step is the medium of a person's effort, and of the advancement that follows in its wake, a higher rank came to be called a *qadam* in a figurative sense. Then that *qadam* — high rank, place of honour — is attributed to صِدْق (*ṣidq*): true, certain, abiding, everlasting. The joining is the whole point. It emphasises that the high rank they were to get was real, certain, established, abiding and everlasting — not something like the ranks and offices of the mortal world. To begin with, it is never certain one would get those at all. If some extra effort does win one of them, its continuity cannot be certain. In fact, what is certain is that these will vanish in time — sometimes within one's own lifetime. And when the time comes to die, one goes empty-handed: all ranks, offices and blessings remain behind. So the sense is: O Prophet ﷺ, give the believers the good news that they will have a perfect place with their Lord — an asset that is certain and lasting.

**Where the scholars differed.** Ibn Kathir states plainly that scholars have differed over the meaning of the reward for good deeds in this ayah, and he lays the views out rather than choosing between them:

- ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said about this ayah: "Eternal happiness has been written for them."
- Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās said: "It is the good reward for what they have done."
- Mujāhid said: "It is their good deeds – their prayers, fasting, charity, and glorification." He then said, "And Muhammad ﷺ will intercede for them."

Ibn Kathir presents these as differing readings, and it is right to leave them as he left them — three ways the earliest authorities understood a promise whose substance all of them affirm.

**Truth in the word ṣidq.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some commentators have said that through the introduction of the word *ṣidq* here an indication has been given: these high ranks can be achieved only through truth and absolute sincerity. Mere verbal claims of having faith and a formal recital of the Kalimah of īmān are not enough, until one embraces the faith truly and duly — verbally, emotionally and intellectually. And such faith invariably results in adherence to good deeds and avoidance of evil ones. The rank promised is real; on this reading, the faith that reaches it must be real too.

## "This is indeed an evident sorcerer"

Ayah 2 closes with the verdict the disbelievers passed: *"This is indeed an evident sorcerer."*

Ibn Kathir's comment is restrained and devastating. They said this although Allah had sent them a Messenger from among themselves, a man of their own race, as a bearer of good news and as a warner. But they are the liars in saying that.

Set the two ends of the passage against each other and the irony is complete. Ayah 1 calls the revelation the Book *rich in wisdom*, verses in which the wisdom of judgment is clear; the objectors called it sorcery. Ayah 2 says Allah sent it through *a man from among themselves*; they said Allah is greater than sending a human Messenger. Ibn Kathir's verdict on that verdict is one word: liars.

## Living it

**Hold your curiosity where Allah placed the limit.** The letters at the head of the sūrah are the first lesson: not everything revealed is meant to be cracked open. Recite them, believe them, and trust that the Prophet ﷺ — mercy personified for the whole world — withheld nothing his community needed.

**Do not measure the message by the messenger's humanity.** The objectors expected a messenger from Allah to be an angel rather than a human being. But a messenger's mission cannot be accomplished without a likeness of kind between him and those he is sent to — so a message for human beings comes through a human being. That is not a defect in the arrangement; it is the whole reason the arrangement works.

**Invest where the place is real.** Everything Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says about worldly rank — uncertain to obtain, uncertain to keep, certain to be left behind at death — is the argument for redirecting effort toward the *qadam ṣidq*: a place with your Lord that is certain and lasting.

**Make your faith the kind that reaches it.** On the reading some commentators gave, *ṣidq* sets the condition: not a claim on the tongue but faith embraced truly and duly — verbally, emotionally and intellectually — which then invariably shows itself in good deeds done and evil ones avoided. And in Mujāhid's account, the very prayers, fasting, charity and glorification you offer today are themselves what the promise refers to.

passages.title: The Creator-Lord and His signs in creation
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out the shape of these verses. Ayah 3: Allah created the heavens, the earth and the whole system of the universe in six days, then took His position on the Throne, and manages all matters. Ayah 4 states the belief in the Hereafter. Ayat 5 and 6 mention signs openly visible — evidences of the perfect power and eloquent wisdom of Allah — an extension of what ayah 3 said briefly.

## Ayah 3: Tawḥīd proved from an undeniable reality

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads ayah 3 as a proof of Tawḥīd (the Oneness of Allah): there is no associate or partner to Allah in the creation of the heavens and the earth, nor in the management and operation of this entire universal system. Once that stands established, how could someone else be made an associate or partner in His pristine Divinity, in worship of Him, or in obedience to Him? Doing so is the highest conceivable injustice.

So the ayah concludes: *"That is Allah, your Lord; so worship Him"* — which Ibn Kathīr explains as worship Him alone with no partners. Then the rebuke, *"Then will you not remember?"*, which Ibn Kathīr addresses to the idolaters: you worship gods alongside Allah **while you know** that He alone is the Creator. He cites their own admission: *"And if you ask them who created them, they will surely say: 'Allah'"* (43:87), and *"Say: Who is Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Great Throne? They will say: 'Allah.' Say: Will you not then have taqwā?"* (23:86–87).

## "In six days"

Ibn Kathīr reports two views: it was said they are like these days of ours, and it was also said that every day is like a thousand years of what we reckon.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the obvious question: a "day" as we know it denotes the time from sunrise to sunset — but the sun did not exist before the creation of the heavens, earth and stars, so how could sunrise and sunset be calculated? What is intended is the *measure of time* used up between sunrise and sunset.

Making this huge world ready and functional can only be attributed to the Being who is purest of the pure and whose power is absolute. When He intends to create He needs no raw materials in advance and no staff to assist; He creates instantly. The six days were never a limitation: it was within His power to create the heavens and the Earth and all they contain in a single instant. That duration was chosen in consideration of His particular wisdom.

## "Then He rose over the Throne" — how the Salaf handled this

Ibn Kathīr says of the ʿArsh (Throne) that it is the greatest of the creatures and is like a ceiling for them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states what stands proved from the Qur'an and Ḥadīth: the Throne of al-Raḥmān is some created object which encompasses the entire heavens, the Earth and the whole universe — and knowing any more about its reality is beyond any human effort. Scientific knowledge in our time is at its zenith, yet scientists still confess that there are stars in the firmament whose light has not yet reached our Earth, though the speed of light is 186,000 miles per second. If that is the graph of human limitations among planets and stars, how could human efforts to find out about the heavens farther and higher be taken as credible — let alone the ʿArsh of al-Raḥmān, above even what is termed the seventh heaven.

**So what do we say about *istawā*?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is clear. Allah, the high and the true, is above and beyond human concepts of body and mass. Neither does His existence relate to any direction or form. How then are we to explain the nature, mode or manner of His establishing Himself on the Throne? Only by saying that this belongs to what the Qur'an's terminology calls *mutashābihāt* — statements of hidden meaning that human reason cannot comprehend. Of these the Qur'an says: *"No one knows its interpretation except Allah. And those well-grounded in knowledge say: 'We believe therein'"* (3:7) — and we do not bother to go digging out its reality.

This is the standard approach in all such matters where Allah has been attributed to a place or form, and wherever words such as hand, face and shank appear for Him in the Qur'an. The ʿaqīdah (belief) of the majority of the ʿulamā of the Muslim Ummah is threefold: **one believes these words to be true in their place; believes that what Allah means by them is correct; and sets aside the concern to know their nature and reality as beyond one's ability to comprehend.** As for the later-day ʿulamā who suggested some meanings, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that they did so only in a degree of probability — *perhaps it may mean this*. And probabilities disclose no reality. So the only simple and straight creed is that of the Ṣaḥābah, the Tābiʿīn and the Salaf, who were satisfied to entrust the reality of such matters to Divine Knowledge.

## "Arranging the affair" — a universe never left alone

*Yudabbiru l-amr.* Ibn Kathīr glosses it: He controls the affairs of the creatures. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: Allah did not, after having created the universe, abandon it to survive on its own; positioned on the Throne, He Himself manages, directs and controls everything, every moment. Ibn Kathīr adds that no affair distracts Him from other affairs, no matter troubles Him, and the persistent requests of His creatures do not annoy Him. He governs big things as He governs small things everywhere — on the mountains, in the oceans, in populated areas, in wastelands. He supports this with *"Not even the weight of a speck of dust escapes His knowledge in the heavens or in the earth"* (34:3); *"And no moving creature is there on earth but its provision is due from Allah"* (11:6); and *"Not a leaf falls but He knows it. There is not a grain in the darkness of the earth, nor anything fresh or dry, but is written in a Clear Record"* (6:59).

**A narration on the awe of this ayah.** Ibn Kathīr relates that ad-Darāwardī narrated from Saʿd bin Isḥāq bin Kaʿb bin ʿUjrah that when this ayah was revealed, they met a great caravan whom they thought should be Arabs and said to them, "Who are you?" They replied, "We are Jinns. We left al-Madīnah because of this ayah." Ibn Kathīr notes it was recorded by Ibn Abī Ḥātim.

## "No intercessor except after His permission"

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the majesty here: even a Prophet and Messenger cannot intercede on behalf of anyone, on his own, before Him — unless Allah Himself grants him the permission to intercede. Ibn Kathīr gathers the parallel verses: *"Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?"* (2:255); *"And there are many angels in the heavens whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah has given leave for whom He wills and is pleased with"* (53:26); and *"Intercession with Him profits not except for him whom He permits"* (34:23).

## Ayah 4: the return, and why it is not hard to believe

Ibn Kathīr: the return of the creatures on the Day of Resurrection is to Him, and He will bring everyone into being as He brought them in the beginning.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān highlights how the ayah argues: the claim — *"Towards Him is the return of you all"* — asserted as *"a real and true promise from Allah"* — then explained through simple logic: *"Surely He originates the creation, then He will bring it again."* There is no sense in worrying about how this entire universe would start pulsating with life after it has been eliminated. The Sacred Power who has the mastery to create something the first time — without any pre-existing matter and without any prototype of form and shape — should hardly find difficulty in creating once again everything He had made and then unmade. Ibn Kathīr cites the Qur'an's own phrasing: *"And He it is Who originates the creation, then He will repeat it; and this is easier for Him"* (30:27).

For those who believed and did deeds of righteousness, Ibn Kathīr says the reward will be *with justice and complete recompense*. For those who disbelieved, they will be punished on the Day of Resurrection by different forms of torment, such as fierce hot winds, boiling water, and the shadow of black smoke. He cites *"Then let them taste it; a boiling fluid and dirty wound discharges. And other torments of similar kind all together!"* (38:57–58) and *"This is the Hell which the criminals denied. They will go between it and the fierce boiling water!"* (55:43–44).

## Ayah 5: made to be looked at

Ibn Kathīr introduces these signs as indicative of Allah's complete power and great might. He made the rays that come forth from the bright sun the source of light, and the beams that come forth from the moon a light — **of two different natures, so they would not be confused with one another** — and made the dominion of the sun in the daytime and the moon in the night.

**Why ḍiyāʾ for the sun and nūr for the moon.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that both words mean glow and light, so many master lexicographers have taken them as synonyms. But al-Zamakhsharī, al-Ṭībī and some others distinguished them: *nūr* is general — whether strong or weak, dim or clear, every light is called nūr — while *ḍawʾ* and *ḍiyāʾ* refer to light that is strong and clear. For the usual business of life the sharp, clear light of day is required, while the comparatively dim light of night is preferred for ordinary chores.

The Qur'an differentiates these lights variously elsewhere: *"And made the moon a light therein, and made the sun a lamp"* (71:16), and *"and placed in it a lamp and a shining moon"* (25:61). Because *sirāj* means lamp, and a lamp's light is its own rather than borrowed, some commentators have said that ḍiyāʾ is a thing's intrinsic light while nūr is extrinsic light derived from something else. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is candid: that semantic approach appears influenced by Greek thought, otherwise it has no lexical basis, and the Qur'an has not given any categorical verdict about it. A separate view from Zajjāj takes *ḍiyāʾ* as the plural of *ḍawʾ* — which, al-Manār suggests, may perhaps indicate the sun being a compendium of the seven colours of light that show up in the post-rain rainbow.

**"And measured out for it stages."** *Qaddarahu* derives from *taqdīr*, which Maʿārif ul Qurʼān defines as maintaining something at the level of a particular quantity and measure in terms of time, place or attributes. The Qur'an uses it for the timings of night and day (73:20), for travel distances (34:18), and for quantitative measures in general (*"and created everything, then determined a measure for it, determining precisely"*, 25:2). *Manāzil* is the plural of *manzil*, which means the place one arrives at on a journey. Allah has appointed specific limits for the movement of the sun and the moon, and each of these is called a manzil.

Ibn Kathīr describes the moon's cycle: it starts small, its light increases until it completes a full moon, then it begins to decrease until it returns to its first phase at the conclusion of the month — *"till it returns like the old dried curved date stalk. It is not for the sun to overtake the moon, nor does the night outstrip the day. They all float, each in an orbit"* (36:39–40). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān counts these stages as thirty or twenty-nine, though since the moon is not visible for at least one day they are usually known as twenty-eight, while the orbit of the sun completes in a year with 360 or 365 stages.

**A grammatical puzzle.** *Qaddarahu* uses a pronoun in the singular — "measured out for **it**" — although the stages of both the sun and the moon are referred to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports two explanations. Some commentators say that although the form is singular, in terms of the reference to each single one it includes both — a usage of which examples abound in the Qur'an and in Arabic idiom. Others say the purpose here is to describe the stages of the moon only, so the pronoun refers back to the moon. The reason: one cannot find out the stages of the sun without instruments and calculations — looking at the sun, nobody can tell whether it is the 8th or the 21st. The moon's states are different every day, and by the end of the month it is simply not visible, so even uneducated people can figure out the dates by observing it. Ibn Kathīr states the division plainly: the days are revealed by the action of the sun, and the months and the years by the moon.

## Living it: keeping the moon's calendar alive

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān turns this into something practical. Because great attention is paid in the injunctions of Islam to ensuring that abiding by them is easy for everyone — educated or uneducated, urbanized or rustic — reliance has usually been placed on the lunar year, month and dates: Ṣalāh, Ṣawm, Ḥajj, Zakāh and ʿiddah.

One may keep the lunar calendar for those obligations and use the solar calendar in commercial and vocational activities. But this is subject to a condition: the lunar calendar must continue to be in use among Muslims on a collective basis, so that the occasions and timings of religious obligations such as Ramaḍān and Ḥajj remain in common knowledge at all times — guarding against the terrible situation in which Muslims know no other months but January, February and so on. Muslim jurists have therefore placed the responsibility of keeping the lunar calendar alive on Muslims as *farḍ al-kifāyah* (collective obligation). And the calendar used in the tradition of the blessed prophets, in the Sunnah of the last of them, the Prophet ﷺ, and in the practice of his rightly-guided Khulafāʾ was no other than this very lunar calendar — so using it is certainly an effective cause of blessings and rewards for Muslims today as well.

## "Allah did not create this except in truth"

Ibn Kathīr: He did not create that for amusement, but with great wisdom and perfect reasoning — as in *"And We created not the heaven and the earth and all that is between them without purpose"* (38:27), and *"Did you think that We had created you in play, and that you would not be brought back to Us?"* (23:115–116). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses over what we are asked to notice: two inexhaustible treasure troves of light, given such ideal measures of movement that we can find the year, the month, the day, its hours, right down to every second. Their movement does not vary; these marvels of Allah’s making need no workshop appointments for repairs, no greasing, no replacement of worn-out parts. Someone in eternity had asked them to move and be good — and this they are doing even today.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the closing words of ayah 5 as an added warning: these are elaborated signs — loud and clear — telling the truth to people blessed with reason and insight.

## Ayah 6: signs for those who have taqwā

Ibn Kathīr: the day and the night alternate, when one arrives the other goes, and so on, **with no errors** — *"He brings the night as a cover over the day, seeking it rapidly"*; *"It is not for the sun to overtake the moon"* (36:40); *"Cleaver of the daybreak; He has appointed the night for resting"* (6:96). And "all that Allah has created in the heavens and the earth" means the signs that indicate His greatness.

There is a shift in the endings. Ayah 5 closes with *"He explains the āyāt in detail for people who have knowledge"* — Ibn Kathīr: He explained the signs and proofs for people who know. Elsewhere the same evidence yields *"signs for men of understanding"* (3:190), which he glosses as intelligent men. But ayah 6 says *"āyāt for those who have taqwā"* — and Ibn Kathīr explains taqwā here as fearing Allah's punishment, wrath and torment.

**Signs of what, exactly?** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān answers on two fronts. That they prove Tawḥīd is not difficult to see: He makes things as no one can, He creates without the help of materials, personnel or prototype, and He has the mastery to operate them under a system that never breaks or must be replaced. That they prove the Hereafter takes one more step: Allah made, in His infinite wisdom, objects of such proportion and efficiency for the benefit of human beings. It is not possible that He would have created human beings — the served ones in this universe — just for nothing, without assigning them any duties. Once it stands settled that restrictions apply to the served one of this universe, it becomes necessary that those who observe them and those who do not should face an accounting of what they have done: the obedient rewarded, the disobedient punished. And plainly things do not work like this in the present world of our experience — it is quite likely that a criminal here lives better than someone righteous, innocent and mindful of Allah. This is what Qiyāmah and the Ākhirah are.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds what these two verses establish together: that the Lord Almighty is fully capable of bringing this universe to an end, reducing it to particles, then reassembling those particles and bringing everything back to life anew — and that when He does so, it will be nothing but reasonable and wise.

**What the passage asks of you.** The sun's strong light, the moon's changing face, the alternation of night and day — elaborated signs that are loud and clear. Ayah 3 names the One who made and manages all of it as your Lord, then names the response: *That is Allah, your Lord; so worship Him.* And ayah 4 tells you the return to Him is a real and true promise.

passages.title: Two destinies: the heedless and the believers
passages.tafsir:
**Two people can look at the same sky and walk away as two different kinds of human being.** The verses just before these four ayat pointed to the heavens and the earth, the sun and the moon — what Maʿārif ul Qurʾān calls "prominent manifestations of Allah's perfect power and wisdom" — and used them to establish the Oneness of Allah and the reality of the Hereafter. Now, says Maʿārif, the Qurʾan reports that "despite such open signs and evidences spread out in this universe, human beings split up in two groups": those who paid no heed and settled down here (ayat 7–8), and those who pondered, believed, acted, and are carried all the way home (ayat 9–10).

The pairing is visible in the Arabic as printed. Ayah 7 opens *inna alladhīna lā yarjūna liqāʾanā* — "Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us" — and ayah 9 opens with the same construction, *inna alladhīna āmanū wa ʿamilū al-ṣāliḥāt*.

## The three marks of the first group

**One: they do not look forward to the meeting.** The phrase *lā yarjūna liqāʾanā* is rendered "do not expect to meet Us." Ibn Kathir describes them as those "who disbelieved in the meeting with Allah on the Day of Resurrection and did not look forward to it" — two things, not one: they neither believed in the meeting nor anticipated it. Maʿārif puts it the same way — "such people did not think that they would meet their Lord. They have forgotten all about the inevitability of their life in the Hereafter."

**Two: they are pleased and at rest with the life of this world.** Ibn Kathir says they were "well-pleased with the life of this world and at rest in it." Al-Hasan, quoted by Ibn Kathir, sharpens this into a sentence worth memorising: *"They adorned it and praised it until they were well pleased with it."* On his wording, contentment with this world is not a mood that simply descends on a person; it is the end of a process the person himself carried out.

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān draws the picture out: "they are sitting there, so satisfied and so content, as if they just do not have to go anywhere else from here. This, to them, was the end of the line." And yet everyone must bid farewell to this world — "so open a truth that no one can go about doubting it." Maʿārif's conclusion follows immediately: "when going away from here is certain, then, some preparation has to be made for the place one is going to."

**Three: they are heedless of Our signs.** Al-Hasan spells this heedlessness out on two levels. They were "heedless of Allah's signs in the universe, they did not contemplate them," and "also heedless of Allah's Laws, for they didn't abide by them." Maʿārif gathers both into a single phrase — they are "continuously heedless to Allah's verses and signs."

## Living below your own rank

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān's commentary here is an argument about human dignity, and it turns "heedlessness" from a vague fault into a specific tragedy. These people, it says, "failed to recognize their creator and master and failed to recognize even themselves" — and the second failure feeds the first. "It never occurred to them that they were no animal like other animals." They never discovered that their Lord had blessed them "with intelligence, reason and commonsense in a degree much higher than that of the animals," or that the whole apparatus of creation had been put at their doorsteps, "as if commissioned to serve them."

From that noticing, Maʿārif says, a chain of reasoning should have followed: this "should have made them realize that there has to be something their Lord would want them to do, some duty or obligation or charge." If there is a charge, "they would have to account for whatever they had been asked to do." And if there is an accounting, "it would be necessary that there should be a day fixed for ultimate reckoning and recompense — known as the day of Qiyāmah or al-Ḥashr (Doomsday, Resurrection) in the terminology of the Qurʾan." On this reading the Hereafter is not an add-on to belief; it is where the logic of being human lands, once you admit you were given more than an animal was given.

"But," Maʿārif concludes, "such people did nothing like that, instead, preferred to live their lives at the level of common animals." That is the charge in ayah 7 as Maʿārif frames it — not that they were wicked beyond measure, but that they were offered a rank and declined it.

The way out was always available and never taken: "Had they pondered over the marvel of the heavens and the earth and what was created in between them and, for that matter, over what was in their own person, they would have understood the reality behind everything and they would have thus come out of their fatal negligence." Two places to look — the sky and the self — and they looked at neither.

## "Their abode will be the Fire, because of what they used to earn"

Ayah 8 delivers the verdict. Al-Hasan's sentence, quoted by Ibn Kathir, runs straight on from ayah 7 into ayah 8 without a break: "Their abode on the Day of Return is Fire, a reward for what they have earned in their worldly life from among their sins and crimes. That is beside their disbelief in Allah, His Messenger and the Last Day."

Maʿārif says the same in a line: the punishment awaiting them "is nothing but the outcome of their own deeds."

## A mirror held up to us

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān refuses to let the reader file these two ayat under "disbelievers, elsewhere, long ago." It says plainly: "How regrettable that the signs of disbelievers and deniers pin-pointed by the Qurʾan are no different as far as our own present condition as Muslims is concerned." Look at our way of life and the pattern of our activities and thoughts, and "no one can come to the conclusion that we have some other concern bothering us except the concerns of this world under our noses" — yet, "despite all that, we sit comfortably believing that we are Muslims, as staunch and true as they come."

Against that it sets the early generations, whose calibre "has become unimaginable for us": people "a look at whose faces would remind one of" Allah and "transmit unmistakably that they feared someone above them and their hearts throbbed with the concern of being accountable to Him." And above them all the Prophet ﷺ himself who, Maʿārif notes, "despite being protected from sins (*maʿṣūm*), lived his blessed life in that state." It appears in Shamāʾil al-Tirmidhī that he ﷺ looked sad and concerned fairly often.

The point is not gloom: it is that a heart genuinely expecting to meet Allah leaves a mark on a life.

## Ayah 9: guided *by* their faith

Now the second group. Maʿārif describes these as the people who "pondered over the signs of the most exalted Allah," and "thereby, they recognized Him, believed in Him and, by acting in accordance with the dictates of their faith, became duty-bound to say and do what was good and right." And since belief is bracketed here with good deeds, Maʿārif notes, the *īmān* of this ayah means "belief that is supported by good deeds."

Maʿārif itself draws the comparison: "It will be recalled that the punishment of the first group was the outcome of their own misdeeds. Here, similar to that, it was said about the reward of the second group (of believers), that they have been blessed with this reward by virtue of their belief."

**"Their Lord will guide them through their faith."** Ibn Kathir gives two readings of *yahdīhim rabbuhum bi-īmānihim* and does not choose between them:

- *Because of* their faith — meaning Allah "will guide them on the Day of Resurrection to the straight path until they pass into Paradise because of their faith in this world."
- *Through* their faith — meaning "their faith will assist them on the Day of Resurrection," as Mujāhid said: **"Their faith will be a light in which they will walk."**

Maʿārif adds a point of vocabulary. The well-known meaning of *hidāyah* is "to tell or show the way"; but "on occasions, it is also used in the sense of taking someone all the way to the desired destination. At this place, this is the meaning intended." And the destination is spelled out by the words that follow: Maʿārif glosses the promise as "take them to their destination, the Jannah, where rivers shall be flowing in the Gardens of Bliss." This is not a Lord who points down the road and leaves you to it. He conducts them to the door.

## Ayah 10: what the people of Paradise say

The ayah does not describe the food of Paradise or its furnishings. It reports what its people *say*. Ibn Kathir: "this is the condition of the people of Paradise." Three utterances, in order — Maʿārif treats them as three states of the life of the people of Jannah.

### *Subḥānaka Allāhumma* — "Glory be to You, O Allah"

First, the word *daʿwāhum*. Maʿārif warns against its familiar sense of "claim, something a plaintiff does against the responding party." Here *daʿwā* is used "in the sense of *duʿāʾ* (prayer, supplication)." So: the duʿāʾ of the people of Jannah, once they have arrived, will take the form of *Subḥānaka Allāhumma* — glorifying the exalted majesty of Allah, "known as Tasbīḥ in the religious terminology of Islam."

Which raises a difficulty, and Maʿārif puts it bluntly: duʿāʾ "is the act of asking for something or the seeking of what one would like to have," and the words "Pure are You, O Allah" have "no element of asking or seeking in them."

The people of Jannah "will have the most comprehensive bliss which will include everything they could wish for almost automatically as they would have wished. So, there will be no asking or seeking." What replaces petition is pure glorification. And it is not the tasbīḥ of duty — "not something like an obligatory act of worship they used to do in their mortal lives (whether or not they enjoyed doing so)." Rather, "they would savor the taste of saying these words of glorification and say *Subḥānaka Allāhumma* on their own, gratefully delighted." Worship, stripped of obligation and of need, turns out to be what the soul does for pleasure.

Maʿārif reinforces this with a ḥadīth qudsī — reported there without naming a collection — in which Allah says that a servant of His "who remains busy glorifying Me all the time, so much so that he finds no time even to ask what was to be asked," will be given "the best of what is asked by all those who ask," his needs taken care of without his having to ask. Which is why Maʿārif concludes that *Subḥānaka Allāhumma* "could also be called a duʿāʾ."

A report carried by Imām Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Mundhir and others (cited via Rūḥ al-Maʿānī and Qurṭubī) adds that when the people of Jannah wish to have something they will say *Subḥānaka Allāhumma*, and hearing this the angels will instantly present what they wished before them — "as if, the words *Subḥānaka Allāhumma* will serve as a password or access code for the people of Jannah through which they will articulate their wish, and the angels, doing their duty, will fulfill it every time."

**And this is not only a Hereafter matter.** It is on this same principle, Maʿārif says, that "a Ḥadīth in the Ṣaḥīḥ of al-Bukhārī and Muslim reports that the Holy Prophet ﷺ used to make the following duʿāʾ when in pain or anxiety":

> *There is no god but Allah, the Great, the Forbearing; there is no god but Allah, the Lord of the Great Throne; there is no god but Allah, the Lord of the Heavens and the Lord of the Earth and the Lord of the Generous Throne.*

Imām al-Ṭabarī said that the righteous forbears of the Muslim community (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥūn*) used to call this the prayer of pain, the *duʿāʾ al-karb*: "whenever in intense pain, anxiety or distress, they would recite these words and pray to Allah for relief" (cited via Tafsīr Qurṭubī). The words ask for nothing; they only declare who Allah is. That is the dunya's version of the speech of Paradise.

### *Salām* — their greeting

*Taḥiyyah*, Maʿārif explains, is "the word used to greet someone coming in or met elsewhere." In the Gardens the greeting is *salām*, and it means: "good news to you that you now stand protected against everything painful or unpleasant."

Who greets them? Maʿārif says the people of Jannah "will be greeted with the word *salām* from Allah Taʿālā or from the angels," and cites both possibilities: "*Salām* — a word from a merciful Lord" (36:58), and "and angels will come to them from every gate [saying] *Salāmun ʿalaykum*" (13:23–24). "There is no contradiction in the two sayings." Ibn Kathir gathers the same family of parallel ayat, adding "Their greeting on the Day they shall meet Him will be *Salām*" (33:44).

And one more shift: in this world *salām* is itself a duʿāʾ — you are asking peace for the person you greet. In Jannah, "where one would have everything one needs or wishes to have, therefore, this word will not retain its sense of prayer there, instead, will become a complement of glad tidings" (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī).

### *Al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn* — the closing word

Ibn Kathir finds in the final phrase "an indication that Allah Almighty is the Praised One always, the Worshipped at all times." This is why "He praised Himself at the beginning and the duration of His creation," and "in the beginning of His Book and the beginning of its revelation" — "All the praises and thanks be to Allah, Who has sent down to His servant the Book" (18:1), "All praise is due to Allah, Who created the heavens and the earth" (6:1). The ayah also indicates, he says, that Allah "is the Praised One in this world and in the Hereafter and in all situations."

He then cites a Ḥadīth recorded by Muslim: **"The people of Paradise will be inspired to glorify Allah and praise Him as they instinctively breathe."** And he explains why this will be their nature: "because of the increasing bounties of Allah upon them. These bounties are repeated and brought back again and increased with no limit or termination." Praise there is not a ritual performed at intervals; it is respiration.

**Why this order?** Maʿārif offers two explanations. First, the two utterances point to two kinds of divine attributes: *Subḥānaka* belongs to "the attributes of being the most exalted which show that He is free from and beyond any shortcoming or evil," while *al-ḥamdu lillāh* belongs to "the attributes of being the noblest which show honor, greatness, magnanimity and perfection." Both are named together at the close of Sūrah al-Raḥmān: "Blessed is the name of your Lord, the Possessor-par-Excellence of Majesty and Honor" (55:78). "Since the attributes of Majesty and Honor follow in that order," the people of Jannah recount His Majesty first and His Honour second.

Second, the three states form a natural sequence: they say *Subḥānaka Allāhumma*; "in response to which, they will receive the greeting of *salām* from Allah Taʿālā, as a result of which, they will say *al-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn*" (Rūḥ al-Maʿānī). A call, an answer, a thanksgiving — a conversation, endlessly renewed.

Maʿārif adds that "the essential aim of the statement is to indicate that the people of Jannah, once there, will start knowing Allah Taʿālā better." It transmits from the spiritual master Shahābuddīn Suhrawardī that after reaching Jannah, "the people of Jannah as a whole will be blessed with a station of knowledge and wisdom which is occupied by ʿUlamāʾ in the mortal world. The ʿUlamāʾ would rise to the station the prophets have here. The prophets would rise to the station occupied by Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ" — who "will occupy the highest station of nearness to Allah in Jannah." Maʿārif suggests it is possible this is *al-maqām al-maḥmūd*, "the praised station," referred to in the duʿāʾ recited after the adhān, in which Muslims pray that their Prophet ﷺ be blessed with it — "a prayer he had himself taught them to make."

## Living it

Al-Qurṭubī, in *Aḥkām al-Qurʾān*, draws a practical rule straight out of ayah 10: "According to this conduct of the people of Jannah, Sunnah in eating and drinking, and in everything else we do, is that one starts with *Bismillāh* and ends at *Alḥamdulillāh*." He cites the Prophet's ﷺ teaching — Maʿārif quotes it without naming a collection — that it is liked by Allah that His servant, "when he eats or drinks something, starts with *Bismillāh* and, when he is finished with it, says *Alḥamdulillāh*."

It is also recommended (*mustaḥabb*) that a person making duʿāʾ close it with the words of this ayah — *wa ākhiru daʿwāhum ani-l-ḥamdu lillāhi rabb al-ʿālamīn* — and al-Qurṭubī adds that "it is better to also recite the following last verses of Sūrah al-Ṣāffāt" (37:180–182), which move through the same three stages: "Pure is your Lord, Lord of all might, above from what they ascribe to Him. And *salām* be on the Messengers. And praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds."

So the passage hands us a diagnosis and a habit. The diagnosis is ayat 7–8: is the meeting with Allah genuinely part of the future you expect; have you been adorning and praising this world until you are pleased with it; do the signs — in creation, and in His Laws — still register? The habit is ayah 10: begin with His name, end with His praise, and let glorification stand where your asking would have been. The people of Paradise will speak this way because they cannot help it; we speak this way now in order to become people who one day cannot help it.

passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about**

The deniers of the Hereafter had dared Allah to bring the threatened punishment forward. These four ayat answer that dare — not by producing the punishment, but by exposing what the demand reveals about the people making it, and what Allah's refusal to hurry reveals about Him.

The argument moves in four steps. First: if Allah answered requests for harm as readily as He answers requests for good, mankind would already be finished. Second: look at what those same people actually do when real harm touches them — and at what they do the moment it lifts. Third: do not mistake the delay for safety, because earlier nations were reckoned with in this very world. Fourth: you are standing on the ground those nations left behind, and the terms of your tenancy are that you are being watched.

Running through all four is Allah's forbearance — His deliberate slowness to punish. Ibn Kathir opens on exactly that note, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān closes on its consequence: this is mercy, not indifference, and the mercy is itself a test.

## The dare, and the mercy that refuses it

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. This verse relates to people who deny the Hereafter, and who, when warned of its punishment, would mockingly say, "if you are telling the truth, bring this punishment now," or something like, "why would this punishment not come soon enough?" Maʿārif ul Qurʼān likens this to what Naḍr ibn Ḥārith had said: "O Allah, if this thing is true, let stones rain down upon us from the heavens, or send some other severe punishment."

The answer comes in the verse itself. Allah is, after all, powerful over everything; He can send the promised punishment instantly, right now. But in His infinite wisdom and mercy He prefers not to. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the sting: when people like these wish evil and hardship on themselves, they do not realise what they are doing. Had Allah been granting their curses on themselves as soon as they wished — as He answers their positive prayers fairly often — "all of them would have been destroyed to the last man."

**Ibn Kathir's angle — this is about you, not only about them.** Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as Allah telling us about His forbearance and benevolence with His servants. He does not respond to them when, during times of grief or anger, they pray with evil intentions against themselves, their wealth or their children. He knows they do not truly intend evil for themselves, so He does not respond — and that non-answer, Ibn Kathir says, "is in reality kindness and mercy." Meanwhile He does respond when they pray for themselves, their wealth and their money with good, blessing and growth. Had He responded to all their evil requests, He would have destroyed them.

Mujāhid put it concretely: "It is the man saying to his son or money when he is angry, 'O Allah don't bless him (or it) and curse him (or it).' Should Allah respond to this man in this request as He responds to him with good, He would destroy them."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same reading through named intermediaries: Ibn Jarīr, on the authority of Qatādah, and al-Bukhārī and Muslim, on the authority of Mujāhid, report that the invoking of a curse here refers to what an angry person sometimes does when he breaks into supplicating that his children, wealth or property be destroyed. Even blurted-out words of curse on these stand included. And Allah, in His infinite mercy, does not hasten to answer such prayers.

So the ayah has two audiences at once. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states this plainly: the main address concerns the deniers of the Hereafter who demanded instant punishment, but in view of its universality it includes Muslims as well, who may break into invoking a curse on themselves, their belongings or their children under some fit of grief or anger. Allah's customary practice with both, because of His grace and compassion, is the same — no instant answer, "so that the erring person gets the opportunity to think it out and rescind."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records that Abu Bakr al-Bazzār reported in his *Musnad* that Jābir said that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "Do not pray against yourselves, do not pray against your children, do not pray against your wealth, for your prayer may coincide with a time of response from Allah and Allah will respond to you."

Ibn Kathir notes that this hadith was also recorded by Abū Dāwūd.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a related point in its own words, with its own citation. It observes that there are occasions when a moment of Divine approval comes in which what one says on the spot is accepted instantly, and therefore the Prophet ﷺ said: "never pray that evil may fall on your children or things you own — lest that time be the time the prayer is to be accepted — and the curse so invoked may stand answered (and activated) all of a sudden (causing you remorse afterwards)." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that this hadith, on the authority of Sayyidnā Jābir, appears in the *Ṣaḥīḥ* of Muslim under the event of the battle of Buwāṭ. (This is a separate report with its own wording; it should not be merged with the one Ibn Kathir cites above.)

Sit with the logic common to both. The danger is not that an angry curse carries weight of its own. The danger is that it might land in the very hour when supplication is answered.

**Two further reports** in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, both from Qurṭubī, show how much mercy surrounds this. On the authority of a hadith narrative — Qurṭubī names no collection, so neither will we — the Prophet ﷺ said that he had prayed to Allah imploring Him not to answer the curse invoked by a friend or relative upon another friend or relative. And Shahr ibn Ḥawshab said he had read that the angels appointed to take care of human needs have been instructed by Allah, in His mercy, not to write down what His servant says in grief or anger.

**The other half of the ayah.** The verse continues: "So We leave those who expect not their meeting with Us, in their trespasses, wandering blindly in distraction." The delay is genuinely offered as room to reconsider — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the respite is given "so that the denier gets the time to think and abstain from his denial," and that whoever cursed himself out of sudden grief, anger or desperation "gets the lease of time to sort out his conduct." But for a man who has already ruled out ever meeting Allah, that same room becomes the space in which he wanders. The gift is unchanged; what differs is what a person does inside it.

## When the harm actually comes

Having exposed the demand, the passage now puts its makers to the test of experience. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls the approach of this verse an eloquent one, aimed at those who denied that Allah is One and that there is a life to come. When conditions are normal, people find time to debate the nature and existence of Allah and the Hereafter; they feel free to ascribe all sorts of partners and associates to His pristine divinity and look to them in the hope that they will respond at the hour of need. But as soon as some major distress overtakes them, these very people — disappointed by the entire range of false gods they had pinned their hopes on — do nothing but call Allah for help. Not simply once, but repeatedly. They have no choice. They must invoke Him.

Hence the three postures in the ayah: *lying on his side, or sitting, or standing.* Ibn Kathir gives the same three — "He prays while standing, sitting or laying down" — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān ties them to a calling that does not stop: "not simply once but repeatedly, lying, sitting, standing."

Ibn Kathir puts alongside it another ayah about the same person: "but when evil touches him, then he has recourse to long supplications" (41:51) — noting that "long supplications" also means *many* supplications. When man suffers adversity he becomes worried and anxious, so he supplicates more.

Then comes the turn. The verb is *marra* — "he passes on." He passes on as if he had never invoked Us for a harm that touched him. Ibn Kathir: when Allah removes his adversity and lifts his distress, "he turns away and becomes arrogant. He goes on as if nothing were wrong with him before."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the doctrinal conclusion, and it is a striking one: those who associate anyone or anything else with Allah in His exclusive domain as the Dispenser of all that His creation needs *do themselves get to experience the demolition of this belief of theirs*. The crisis refutes it in their own mouths. Yet because of their hostility and obstinacy, they keep glued to their false notion.

**"The wasteful."** The ayah ends: "Thus it is made fair seeming to *al-musrifīn* — the wasteful — that which they used to do." Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah criticising and condemning those who have these qualities or act this way. Squandering is the right image: they were handed the clearest evidence of who actually answers, and threw it away.

**But there is an exception, and a counter-portrait.** Ibn Kathir immediately names those on whom Allah has bestowed good guidance and support, quoting (in the source's own rendering) "Except those who have patience believe and do righteous good deeds" (11:11). And he gives the shape of that life in the words of the Prophet ﷺ — the source relays them without naming a collection, so neither will we:

> "How wonderful is the case of a believer; there is good for him in everything and this is not the case with anyone except a believer. If prosperity attends him, he expresses gratitude to Allah, and that is good for him. And if adversity befalls him, he endures it patiently and that is also good for him."

Set the two portraits side by side and the passage's moral geometry appears. The man of this ayah has two settings — panic and forgetfulness — and neither profits him. The believer also meets two states, but his response to each (gratitude, patience) turns both to gain.

## Why the delay is not a reprieve

The next ayah presses the same subject from a different angle, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes. Let no one miscalculate that punishment cannot come in this world just because Allah gives respite to those who deny and disbelieve. The history of past peoples shows that different kinds of punishments have visited them, because of their obstinacy and disobedience, right here in this world.

Ibn Kathir frames it as an admonition: Allah tells us what happened to past generations when they belied the Messengers and the clear signs and proofs those Messengers brought to them. Notice the ayah's own care on this point — "while their Messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they were not such as to believe." The destruction came after wrongdoing, and after evidence, and after a settled refusal. It was requital, not caprice: "Thus do We requite the people who are criminals."

**A qualification that must be handled carefully.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that Allah has promised that no mass punishment will come upon the Muslim ummah, in consideration of the honour of Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, the foremost among the prophets. But it then makes two hard observations. First, it is in the face of this very merciful indulgence that people have become audacious enough to come forward and invite, even demand, Divine punishment — which is exactly the audacity the passage opened with. Second, indifference to Divine punishment is not proper under any condition, even for Muslims: the promise concerning mass punishment upon the ummah, or the world as a whole, certainly stands, "but the coming of such punishment on particular individuals and nations is possible even now."

## The ground you inherited

From the fate of those nations the passage turns to the people standing on their land: "Then We made you *khalāʾif* in the land after them, that We might see how you would work." *Khalāʾif* is rendered "successors" by Ibn Kathir and "vice-regents" in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: those who come after and take over the place of the ones who are gone. Ibn Kathir puts it directly — Allah made this nation successors after those generations, and sent to them a Messenger, to test their obedience to Him and their following of His Messenger.

The stated purpose of the succession is observation: *li-nanẓura kayfa taʿmalūn*, "that We might see how you would work." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will not let the reader mistake the gift for a reward: after the destruction of past peoples, "We made you successors to them giving you the vice-regency of the earth. But, let this not give you any false idea that this vice-regency of the earth has been given to you so that you could have a good time." The honour was bestowed to test you — "would you learn your lesson from the history of past peoples or would you lose your head drunk with power and wealth?" Its conclusion is worth memorising: worldly power is not something to be proud of or arrogant about; it is "responsibility at its toughest, a charge very heavy and very fragile to handle."

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir cites that Muslim recorded that Abū Naḍrah reported from Abū Saʿīd that Allah's Messenger ﷺ said:

> "The world is indeed sweet and green; and verily Allah is going to install you generations after generations in it in order to see how you act. So safeguard yourselves against the world and avoid (the trial caused by) women. For the first trial of the Children of Israel was due to women."

That hadith is essentially this ayah in the Prophet's ﷺ own idiom — *sweet and green* names the attractiveness, and the very next words turn it into a warning.

**How this ayah was heard.** Ibn Kathir relates that Ibn Jarīr reported, from ʿAbd al-Raḥmān, from Ibn Abī Laylā, that ʿAwf bin Mālik said to Abū Bakr: "In a dream, I saw a rope hanging from the sky and Allah's Messenger ﷺ was being raised. The rope was suspended again and Abū Bakr was raised. Then people were given different measurements around the Minbar, and ʿUmar was favoured with three forearm measurements." ʿUmar's reaction at the time was blunt: "Keep your dream away from us, we have no need for it."

When ʿUmar succeeded, he called for ʿAwf and said, "Tell me about your dream." ʿAwf said, "Do you need to hear about my dream now? Did you not scold me before?" The report gives the explanation of that earlier refusal: "Woe unto you! I hated for you to announce it to the successor of Allah's Messenger ﷺ himself." Read plainly, that is a man who would not have his own future advertised over the head of Abū Bakr.

So ʿAwf related his dream until he got to the three forearms, and said: "One that he was Khalīfah, second he did not — for the sake of Allah — fear the blame of blamers, and third he was a martyr."

At this point in the report Ibn Kathir places the ayah itself — "Then We made you successors after them, generations after generations in the land, that We might see how you would work" — and the account continues: "Then he said: 'Son of the mother of ʿUmar, you have been appointed as Khalīfah, so look at what you will do! About not fearing the blame of blamers, that is Allah's will. About becoming a martyr, how can ʿUmar reach that when the Muslims are in support of him?'"

Three items of glad tidings, and the response takes the first as a summons to account, the second as something not his to claim, the third as beyond his reach. That is what it looks like to hear this ayah as it was meant to be heard.

## Living it

**Guard your tongue when you are angry.** This is the most concrete instruction in the passage, and both sources converge on it: do not pray against yourself, your children, or your wealth. The reason they give is not that the words carry power of their own, but that the moment may be one of answering. If it has already escaped you, the mercy described here is that Allah does not let such invocations be implemented instantly, precisely so that the erring person gets the opportunity, in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's words, "to think it out and rescind." Take it back.

**Reverse the pattern of the second ayah.** What is condemned there is not calling on Allah in distress — that is right and inevitable — but passing on once relief arrives, "as if nothing were wrong with him before." The remedy is to be as insistent in duʿāʾ when nothing is wrong as you were when everything was.

**Do not read delay as approval.** The third ayah exists to close that door. Respite is space to reconsider, not evidence of safety — and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful to say that punishment upon particular individuals and nations remains possible even now.

**Hold whatever you have been given as a charge.** Succession on the earth comes in every scale — a household, a job, wealth, authority. The land you stand on belonged to someone else before you, the honour was given "to test you and to see how you would act," and the terms of your tenancy are that you are being watched.

passages.title: Demanding a different Qur'an from the Prophet
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The chiefs of the Quraysh, hearing the Qur'an recited plainly to them, made a proposal: bring us a different Qur'an, or else change this one. These three ayat are Allah's answer, and they hold together as a single reply built in three moves — the Prophet ﷺ has no authority to change what was not his word (ayah 15); the forty years he had already lived among them before this revelation are themselves the argument for where it came from (ayah 16); and inventing words in Allah's name, or denying His words when they come, is the gravest wrong a person can commit (ayah 17).

## The request behind the request

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains what was actually driving the demand. These were people, it says, who did not know much about Allah, or Revelation, or the prophets He sends. They took prophets to be like common human beings with nothing special about them — and so, of the Qur'an that reached the world through the Prophet of Islam ﷺ, they thought that even this was spoken and written by him.

And there were specific things they wanted removed. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets out their complaint almost as a speech: as for this Qur'an, it is against our beliefs and ideas. The idols our forefathers have worshipped since ever as the providers of their needs — the Qur'an calls them totally false and ineffectual. Things we have long been using and transactions we have long been making — the Qur'an says they are all unlawful. And then it tells us we have to live again after we die and account for everything we have done. All of this makes no sense to us and we are not ready to accept it. So do one of two things: either replace this one with another Qur'an that does not have these things, or at the least amend this very Qur'an and expunge those things from it.

That is why their demand in ayah 15 comes in two tiers: **"Bring us a Qur'an other than this, or change it."** Ibn Kathir reads the second option the same way — they wanted the Prophet ﷺ to take back this Book and bring them another book of a different style, or to change it to a different form. If total replacement was too much to ask, they would settle for editing.

**Notice who is speaking.** Ayah 15 does not simply say "the disbelievers said." It identifies them as *those who hope not for their meeting with Us* — people who do not expect to stand before Allah. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān frames all three ayat as the refutation of a false notion entertained by "the deniers of Ākhirah," the deniers of the life to come, together with the rejection of an inappropriate request they made. Ibn Kathir, for his part, opens the passage by describing these men as the obstinate disbelievers of the Quraysh, who were opposed to the message and denied Allah.

## "It is not for me to change it"

The answer the Prophet ﷺ is told to give is startling in its self-effacement:

> قُلْ مَا يَكُونُ لِي أَنْ أُبَدِّلَهُ مِن تِلْقَاءِ نَفْسِي
> *Say: "It is not for me to change it on my own accord."*

Ibn Kathir's gloss is one line and it settles everything: "This means that it is not up to me to do such a thing. **I am but a servant who receives commands. I am a Messenger conveying from Allah.**" The Prophet ﷺ is the Qur'an's recipient and its carrier, not its owner. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point: the Qur'an was not his Word, nor could he change it on his own; he only followed what was revealed to him by Allah.

Then the ayah goes further than a statement of authority — it goes to fear:

> إِنْ أَتَّبِعُ إِلَّا مَا يُوحَىٰ إِلَيَّ ۖ إِنِّي أَخَافُ إِنْ عَصَيْتُ رَبِّي عَذَابَ يَوْمٍ عَظِيمٍ
> *"I only follow that which is revealed unto me. Verily, I fear the torment of the Great Day if I were to disobey my Lord."*

Ibn Kathir identifies "the Great Day" as the Day of Resurrection. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the logic: if he were to make the least change in it on his own and by his own choice, he would be committing a grave sin, and he feared the punishment that falls upon those who disobey Allah — therefore he could not do it.

Read that against the audience. Men who are described as not hoping for their meeting with Allah are asking a man who says he fears the torment of that very Day to alter Allah's words. And notice the terms in which he answers: *"if I were to disobey my Lord."* The relationship he names is that of a servant to his Lord — which is exactly how Ibn Kathir glosses his position: *I am but a servant who receives commands.*

## The forty years already lived

Ayah 16 turns from refusal to evidence. Ibn Kathir titles this section "The Evidence of the Truthfulness of the Qur'an," and says that Muhammad ﷺ then argued with supporting evidence for the truthfulness of what he had brought them. Two arguments follow, packed into one ayah.

**First: the recitation itself is by Allah's will.** *"Say: 'If Allah had so willed, I should not have recited it to you nor would He have made it known to you.'"* Ibn Kathir says this indicates that he brought this only with the permission and will of Allah for him to do so. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān extends the thought: had it been the will of Allah that this Word should not be recited to them, he would neither have recited it to them nor would Allah have let them know about it. And now that it is the very will of Allah that they be made to listen to precisely that Word — *who can dare make any addition or deletion therein?* Their request is not merely declined; it is pressed back at them as a question they cannot answer.

**Second, and this is the argument that lands:**

> فَقَدْ لَبِثْتُ فِيكُمْ عُمُرًا مِّن قَبْلِهِ ۚ أَفَلَا تَعْقِلُونَ
> *"Verily, I have stayed among you a lifetime before this. Have you then no sense?"*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the argument as if the Prophet ﷺ were speaking directly: just think for a moment — is it not that, much before the revelation of the Qur'an, I spent a long period of forty years of my life among you? During that period you never heard me composing and reciting poetry or writing essays in prose. Had I been proficient in saying something like this Word of Allah, I would naturally have said at least some of it during those forty years. In addition to that, you have direct experience of my character and conduct, particularly of my truth and honesty, during these long forty years of my life among you. You know that I never lied then. How and why would I start lying now after all those forty years?

Ibn Kathir makes the same case: the proof was that he had not fabricated it himself, that they were incapable of refuting it, and that they should be fully aware of his truthfulness and honesty since he grew up among them until Allah sent the Message to him — the Prophet ﷺ was never criticised for anything or held in contempt. Then comes the closing rebuke, *"Have you then no sense?"*, which Ibn Kathir paraphrases as: don't you have brains with which you may distinguish the truth from falsehood?

## Testimony about the years before prophethood

Ibn Kathir supports this with two reports about the Prophet's ﷺ life before his claim. (He relates these, and the accounts further below, without naming a collection for them, so they are given here as he gives them.)

**Heraclius and Abū Sufyān.** When Heraclius, the Roman king, asked Abū Sufyān and those in his company about the Prophet ﷺ, he said: "Have you ever accused him of telling lies before his claim?" Abū Sufyān replied: "No." Ibn Kathir points out what makes this so weighty — Abū Sufyān was then the head of the disbelievers and the leader of the idolators, and still he admitted the truth. It is a clear and irrefutable testimony precisely because it came from the enemy. Heraclius then said: "I wondered how a person who does not tell a lie about others could ever tell a lie about Allah."

**Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib before the Negus.** Jaʿfar said to An-Najāshī, the king of Ethiopia: "Allah has sent to us a Messenger that we know his truthfulness, ancestral lineage, and honesty. He stayed among us before the prophethood for forty years."

Both rest on the same foundation as ayah 16: a life lived in full view, before any claim was ever made.

## A rule for our own lives

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses here for what it calls an *Important Note*, and it is worth taking seriously. This argument of the Qur'an, it says, provides a perfect proof of its veracity as the Word of Allah — but it has also given us a standing rule of conduct in matters of common interest, where we must be able to separate the genuine from the counterfeit and the true from the false. When an office or rank of responsibility has to be given to someone, it becomes necessary to assess that person's qualification and capability, and the best rule for doing so is to go through the record of their past life. If the person is found to be true and trustworthy, the same can be expected of them in future. And if there is no evidence of honesty and truth in that person's past, trusting them for the future just because of what they say or claim is not a wise thing to do.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then applies this with some sharpness: in our time, finding the right person for an office of responsibility has become a nightmare. All sorts of errors — of intent, of background research, of decision-making — are being committed, and those errors are compounded by widespread disorder in social and governmental institutions. The real reason all this is happening, it says, is the abandonment of this natural principle in favour of what is customary, formal, or straight dishonest.

## Ayah 17: the greatest wrong, cutting both ways

> فَمَنْ أَظْلَمُ مِمَّنِ افْتَرَىٰ عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا أَوْ كَذَّبَ بِآيَاتِهِ ۚ إِنَّهُ لَا يُفْلِحُ الْمُجْرِمُونَ
> *"So who does more wrong than he who forges a lie against Allah or denies His Āyāt? Surely, the criminals will never be successful."*

The question is rhetorical — *who could possibly be worse?* — and it names two crimes, each the mirror image of the other. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this final ayah emphasises the subject conclusively, warning that attributing to Allah any statement that was not His Word, or denying what actually was His Word, are both crimes deserving severe punishment.

Ibn Kathir spells out the first half: no one is more wrong, unjust and arrogant than he who invented a lie against Allah, forged claims about Allah, or claimed that Allah had sent a message to him when his claim was not true. And he closes on the second half: no one is more unjust than he who belies the truth which the Messengers have brought supported with evidence and proof. It is worth holding that second sentence alongside how Ibn Kathir opened the passage — with the Quraysh chiefs described as people who were opposed to the message and denied Allah.

**Allah never leaves a claimant unmarked.** Ibn Kathir states a principle here worth holding on to: liars cannot be confused with Prophets. Anyone who makes such a claim — whether lying or telling the truth — will necessarily be supported by Allah with proofs and signs of his falsehood or his truthfulness. Truth is not left without evidence, and fraud is not left without its tell. Ibn Kathir says the difference between Muhammad ﷺ and Musaylamah the liar was clearer to those who met both of them than the difference between forenoon and midnight when it is extremely dark, and that those who are clear-sighted can distinguish, by signs and proofs, between the truthfulness of Muhammad ﷺ and the falsehood of Musaylamah the liar, Sajāh and Al-Aswad Al-ʿAnsī. *(A note for the reader: Ibn Kathir names these last two alongside Musaylamah without further description; the passage tells us only that they too were false claimants whom clear-sighted people could tell apart from the Prophet ﷺ.)*

He then gives three illustrations of that principle in action.

**A man who recognised truth by sight.** ʿAbdullāh ibn Salām said: "When Allah's Messenger ﷺ arrived at Al-Madinah, people were scared away and I was one of them. But when I saw him, I realised that his face could never be the face of a liar." And the first thing he heard from him was a call to spread the greetings of peace, to feed others, to be dutiful to relatives, and to offer prayers in the night when others are asleep — so that you will enter Paradise in peace. The first words he heard were not a claim about the speaker at all, but a call to greeting, generosity, kinship and prayer.

**A man who recognised truth by questioning.** Ḍimām ibn Thaʿlabah came to Allah's Messenger ﷺ and asked him in the presence of his people, Banū Saʿd ibn Bakr: Who raised this heaven? "Allah." And who erected these mountains? "Allah." Who spread out this earth? "Allah." Then: I ask you in the name of the One who raised the heavens, erected the mountains and spread out this earth — has Allah sent you as a Messenger to all mankind? He said, *"By Allah, yes!"* Ḍimām then asked him about ṣalāh, zakāh, ḥajj and fasting; with every question he swore by Allah, and with every response the Prophet ﷺ swore also. Ḍimām then said: "You indeed are telling the truth. By the One Who sent you with the truth I will not increase or decrease from what you have told me." Ibn Kathir notes that this man was content with the few responses of the Prophet ﷺ — he was convinced of his truthfulness by the signs that he himself saw and witnessed. Set that beside the Quraysh chiefs of ayah 15, among whom he had lived for forty years, and who still asked for a different book.

**A man who recognised falsehood while still an idolator.** ʿAmr ibn al-ʿĀṣ, who was not a Muslim at the time and was a friend of Musaylamah, went to him. Musaylamah asked what had been revealed to "your friend" — meaning Allah's Messenger ﷺ — during that period. ʿAmr replied that he had heard his companions reading a short but great sūrah, and recited *"By al-ʿAṣr. Verily, man is in loss…"* (103:1–2) to the end of the sūrah. Musaylamah thought for a while and said that something similar had been revealed to him too — then produced: "O Wabr, O Wabr! You are only two ears and a breast. The rest of you is hollow. What do you think, ʿAmr?" ʿAmr said: "By Allah, you know that I know that you are a liar."

Ibn Kathir's comment is the point of the whole story: this was a statement made by an idolator in judgment of Musaylamah. He knew Muhammad ﷺ and his truthfulness; he also knew Musaylamah and his tendency toward falsehood and lying. And, Ibn Kathir adds, people who think and have insight know even better. Put the two texts side by side and the counterfeit collapses on contact — which is what ayah 16 was inviting the Quraysh to do with their own faculties: *have you then no sense?*

Ibn Kathir also sets alongside this the parallel ayah of Sūrat al-Anʿām: *"And who does more aggression and wrong than he who invents a lie against Allah or rejects His Āyāt"* (6:93), placing it directly next to our ayah.

## What it asks of us
