The passage closes with *"Surely, the criminals will never be successful."* Whatever such people hoped to keep — their idols, their long-standing dealings, their freedom from having to account for what they had done — the door of real success is shut against them.

Three things to carry away, all of them inside the text:

**No one may add to the Book or delete from it — the one who received it least of all.** The Prophet ﷺ himself was told to say *"it is not for me to change it on my own accord,"* and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the point home with its own question: now that it is the very will of Allah that this Word be heard, *who can dare make any addition or deletion therein?* The Quraysh wanted three things gone: the falseness of their idols, the lawfulness of their long-standing dealings restored, and the reality of resurrection and accounting dropped. When our own reading of a verse is pulled by our habits, our profits or our inherited practice, that is the pull ayah 15 refuses.

**Judge people by the record, not the claim.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān took the forty-year argument and turned it into a rule for daily life: assess a person for responsibility by the record of their past conduct, not by what they say about themselves. It works because it is how Allah Himself argued in ayah 16.

**Live so that your past can be your evidence.** The Prophet's ﷺ argument before his bitterest opponents was simply the life they had already watched him live — a life in which, as Ibn Kathir says, he was never criticised for anything or held in contempt, and about which the leader of the idolators, asked directly, could not allege a single lie.

passages.title: Powerless intercessors and demands for a sign
passages.tafsir:
**These three ayat answer one question: who, or what, can actually help you before Allah?** The idolaters held two positions that look unrelated but sit side by side here — they kept objects beside Allah and called them their intercessors (ayah 18), and they demanded that Allah send down a sign of their own choosing (ayah 20). Both are answered by pointing back to what belongs to Allah alone: His knowledge in ayah 18, and the Unseen in ayah 20. Ayah 19 sits between the two and delivers the historical verdict: none of this is original. Humanity began as one community, and shirk — associating partners with Allah — is the newcomer.

## "These are our intercessors with Allah" (ayah 18)

The ayah first describes what they worship: **مَا لَا يَضُرُّهُمْ وَلَا يَنفَعُهُمْ** — "that which neither harms them nor benefits them."

Ibn Kathir spells out how empty these objects are. Allah reproaches those who worshipped others beside Him, thinking those gods would intercede for them before Allah; and Allah states that these gods do not harm or benefit, that they have no authority over anything, and that they own nothing. They can never do what the idolaters claimed of them.

Then comes the reply the Prophet ﷺ is told to give:

**قُلْ أَتُنَبِّئُونَ اللَّهَ بِمَا لَا يَعْلَمُ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَلَا فِي الْأَرْضِ**
"Say: Do you inform Allah of that which He knows not in the heavens and on the earth?"

Ibn Jarir explains the meaning as: "Are you telling Allah about what may not happen in the heavens and earth?" The question is put as a rebuke. They are not simply holding a wrong opinion; they are presenting to Allah, as though it were news, something that has no place in His knowledge of the heavens and the earth.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the ayah just before this passage (ayah 17) had already emphasised the subject conclusively, warning that attributing to Allah any statement that was not His Word, or denying what actually was, are crimes deserving severe punishment. That is the setting into which the sentence "these are our intercessors with Allah" falls.

The passage does not end in argument but in glorification: **سُبْحَانَهُ وَتَعَالَىٰ عَمَّا يُشْرِكُونَ**. Ibn Kathir's text continues that Allah then announced that His Glorious Self is far above their shirk and their kufr — their associating partners with Him, and their disbelief. The refutation finishes by lifting the eyes away from the idols altogether.

## Shirk is the newcomer, not worship of Allah alone (ayah 19)

**وَمَا كَانَ النَّاسُ إِلَّا أُمَّةً وَاحِدَةً فَاخْتَلَفُوا** — "Mankind were but one community, then they differed."

Ibn Kathir titles this section bluntly: *Shirk is New*. It was not in existence in the beginning. People were believers in one religion, and that religion was Islam — submission to Allah alone. He cites Ibn ʿAbbas: there were ten centuries between Adam and Nuh, and they were all upon Islam. Then differences among people took place, and they worshipped idols and rivals. So Allah sent extensive evidence and irrefutable proof with His Messengers — as in His words, *so that those who were to be destroyed might be destroyed after a clear evidence, and those who were to live might live after a clear evidence* (8:42).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says the same, citing Tafsir Mazhari: the progeny of Adam (peace be upon him) was essentially a single community of monotheists in the earlier stages of man's presence in the world; shirk and kufr were unknown as such. That state prevailed up to the time of Nuh (peace be upon him), and it was in his time that shirk and kufr showed up — he was the one who had to confront it first.

This reframes everything. Idolatry is not humanity's natural starting point that revelation later corrected. It is a departure that arrived late, and the Messengers were sent with evidence and proof after it arrived.

## What "one community" means — and what it refuses to mean

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a long and pointed lesson here. Between Adam and Nuh (peace be upon them both) is a long period of time. The human race had multiplied and the population had spread out in the world. Differences of colour, ethnicity and social lifestyles were natural; people spreading into different regions would certainly have generated differences on the basis of country and homeland; it is also possible that spoken languages became somewhat different.

And yet — this is the point — the Qur'an did not allow these natural genealogical or tribal differences, or those of colour and country, to become impediments to the grand design of one community. It did not declare the progeny of Adam (peace be upon him) to be different nations and communities because of them. It gave them the status of one community.

Only one thing was allowed to divide them. When kufr and shirk spread out and posed a threat to true belief, then the disbelievers and idolaters were declared a separate community of people — and that, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, is what is indicated by the single word **فَاخْتَلَفُوا**, "then they differed." It supports this with another ayah: *He is the One who created you; yet among you is a disbeliever and among you is a believer* (64:2). What separates the children of Adam into different peoples is deviation from faith and Islam; bonds of lineage or country do not make people separate.

From this Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a conclusion about modern nationalism: bracketing human beings into different groups on the basis of language, homeland, colour or race is, in its words, "ignorance dished out in the garb of enlightenment." It is new — but everything new is not necessarily true and wise; it might as well be the exact opposite of what is wise. It observes that many educated people today have fallen into this narrow concept of nationalism, warns that ordering social life this way is fraught with the seeds of countless unseen disasters, and closes with a prayer that Allah keep the Muslims safe from its evil effects.

## Why judgment has not already fallen

**وَلَوْلَا كَلِمَةٌ سَبَقَتْ مِن رَّبِّكَ** — "and had it not been for a Word that went forth before from your Lord."

Ibn Kathir gives two things this decreed Word means. First, Allah had decreed that He would not punish anyone until the evidence is established against them. Second, He had given His creatures a respite until a defined term had passed. Were it not for that, He would have judged among them in what they disputed — and would have caused the believers to be happy and delighted and the disbelievers to be miserable and wretched.

So the fact that the dispute is still open is not neglect. It is a decree: evidence established first, a respite until a fixed term, then judgment.

## "Why has no sign been sent down to him?" (ayah 20)

Ibn Kathir calls them stubborn, lying disbelievers when they asked why a sign was not revealed to the Prophet ﷺ from his Lord. They meant a sign such as was given to Salih — Allah sent the she-camel to Thamud. Concretely, they wanted Allah to change the mount of As-Safa into gold, or to remove the mountains of Makkah and replace them with gardens and rivers.

Ibn Kathir's answer has two halves. **Allah is capable of doing all of that** — but He is All-Wise in His actions and statements. He cites *Blessed be He Who, if He wills, will assign you better than all that — Gardens under which rivers flow, and will assign you palaces. Nay, they deny the Hour, and for those who deny the Hour We have prepared a flaming Fire* (25:10–11). And he cites *nothing stops Us from sending the Ayat but that the people of old denied them* (17:59).

That second ayah opens onto something remarkable. Ibn Kathir explains Allah's way of dealing with His creatures: He would give to them if they asked things from Him — but if they then did not believe, He would expedite punishment for them. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was given the choice between the people being given what they requested, with punishment to follow if they did not believe, or their request not being answered immediately. **He ﷺ chose the latter.** So the sign they never received was withheld by his choice — and withheld along with it was the punishment that would have followed their refusal to believe.

## "The Unseen belongs only to Allah"

**فَقُلْ إِنَّمَا الْغَيْبُ لِلَّهِ** — Ibn Kathir explains that this means the matter in its entirety is for Allah; He is well aware of the outcome of all matters. Whether a sign comes, and when, is not the Messenger's to decide.

**فَانتَظِرُوا إِنِّي مَعَكُم مِّنَ الْمُنتَظِرِينَ** — "so wait; I am with you among those who wait." The sense Ibn Kathir gives: if you would not believe unless you witness what you asked for, then wait for Allah's judgement — for me, as well as for yourselves. There is no anxiety in the reply and no bargaining. The Prophet ﷺ is told to step calmly into the same waiting and let Allah decide.

## They had already been shown more than they asked for

Ibn Kathir then notes what makes the demand hollow: they had witnessed some of the signs and miracles of the Prophet ﷺ which were even greater than what they had asked for. In their presence he ﷺ pointed to the moon when it was full and it split into two parts, one part behind the mountain and the other before them.

So the request was never a request for evidence. Ibn Kathir puts it precisely: if they had been seeking guidance and firm knowledge by asking for signs, Allah would have known that and would have granted what was requested. But Allah knew that it was their obstinacy that was behind their request, and that none of them would believe. Therefore He left them to suffer in their suspicion and doubt.

He gathers the Qur'an's own verdicts on this kind of heart:

- *Truly, those against whom the Word of your Lord has been justified will not believe — even if every sign should come to them* (10:96–97).
- *And even if We had sent down unto them angels, and the dead had spoken unto them, and We had gathered together all things before their very eyes, they would not have believed, unless Allah willed* (6:111).
- *And even if We opened to them a gate from the heaven…* (15:14), and *if they were to see a piece of the heaven falling down…* (52:44).
- *And even if We had sent down unto you a Message written on paper so that they could touch it with their hands, the disbelievers would have said: this is nothing but obvious magic* (6:7).

Ibn Kathir's conclusion is severe and clarifying: such people do not deserve to have their requests answered, for there is no benefit in answering them; they are obstinate and stubborn as a result of their corruption and immorality. Hence the closing instruction stands unchanged — *so wait; I am with you among those who wait.*

## Living it

**Audit what you lean on.** Ayah 18 gives a test with three parts: does the thing you turn to actually harm, actually benefit, actually own or control anything? Ibn Kathir's answer for the idols was no on every count — no harm, no benefit, no authority, no ownership. Applied honestly, that test cuts through a great deal of what people quietly rely on for rescue.

**Be careful how you speak about Allah.** The rebuke in ayah 18 lands on a sentence — "these are our intercessors with Allah" — and the reply is a question about Allah's own knowledge. Claims about what Allah accepts, arranges or permits are not casual conversation.

**Do not let your community be defined by anything except faith.** Ayah 19, as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads it, held humanity together across colour, land and language, and separated it only along belief. It treats race- and homeland-based nationalism as ignorance in the garb of enlightenment, whatever modern prestige it enjoys.

**Recognise a demand for proof that is really a refusal to submit.** The men of ayah 20 had watched the moon split and still wanted As-Safa turned to gold. Allah knew obstinacy lay behind the request, and knew that none of them would believe. The honest response to doubt is to weigh the evidence already given, not to set Allah a test.

**Treat the delay as respite, not indifference.** Ibn Kathir's reading of ayah 19 is that judgment is held back by a decreed Word — evidence established first, a respite until a defined term. That term is running now.

passages.title: Human fickleness in relief and in the storm
passages.tafsir:
**What holds these three ayat together.** They trace one movement of the human heart from beginning to end: distress, a desperate and utterly sincere turning to Allah, rescue — and then, once the danger has passed, forgetfulness and transgression. Ayah 21 states the pattern as a general truth about people; ayah 22 turns it into an unforgettable scene at sea; ayah 23 shows the aftermath on dry land and tells the reader exactly who pays for it.

## Ayah 21: mercy after hardship, and what people do with it

"And when We let mankind taste mercy after some adversity has afflicted them, behold! They take to plotting against Our Ayat!" (*Ayat* here means the signs of Allah — His verses and the evidences of Him in the world.)

Ibn Kathir explains what "mercy after adversity" looks like: the coming of mercy after distress is like the coming of ease after hardship, fertility after barren years, and rain after drought. These are the ordinary reversals of life — the thing that was closed opening again.

And what happens then? Ibn Kathir cites **Mujahid**, who said that this attitude of man amounts to a mockery and a belying of blessings: the favour arrives and, instead of being received as a sign, it is laughed off or denied.

Ibn Kathir links this to the description a few ayat earlier in the same surah: "And when harm touches man, he invokes Us, lying on his side, or sitting or standing" (10:12) — that is, in every posture, without pause, as long as the pain lasts.

### The hadith of the morning rain

Ibn Kathir brings here a hadith recorded by **Al-Bukhari**. Rain had fallen during the night; the Messenger of Allah ﷺ led the Subh (Dawn) prayer and then asked, "Do you know what your Lord has said last night?" They replied, "Allah and His Messenger know better." He ﷺ said that Allah said: "This morning, some of My servants have become believers and some disbelievers in Me. He who said: 'We have had this rainfall due to the grace and mercy of Allah' is a believer in Me and a disbeliever in the stars. And he who said 'we have had this rainfall due to the rising of such and such star' is a disbeliever in Me and a believer in the stars."

Notice how exactly this fits the ayah. The mercy has just arrived — rain, which Ibn Kathir named as one of the very examples of mercy after distress — and in the same night two hearts divide over the identical blessing. One says *Allah gave this*; the other assigns it to a cause with no Lord behind it. The blessing itself did not decide who they were; what they said about the blessing did. This is "plotting against Our signs" in its most everyday form: receiving the sign and then crediting it to something else.

### "Allah is more swift in planning" — the word *makr*

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** pauses on the word *makr* in this ayah, because it is easily mistranslated. *Makr* in Arabic means a secret plan or move, and it can be good or bad. Wherever the word has passed into a local language carrying only its ugly sense, Maʿārif cautions that care must be taken not to render it as "deception" — in Urdu, the original language of that commentary, it means just that, and Allah is obviously far above any such thing. English, its translator notes, has no such problem: the open sense of *makr* comes through straightforwardly as "plan" or "move."

So the ayah is not describing Allah as a deceiver. It is telling us that against every hidden human move stands a move of Allah's that is swifter.

What does that mean concretely? Ibn Kathir explains: Allah is more capable of gradually seizing them with punishment while granting them the concession of a delay, until the criminals think they will not be punished at all. They mistake respite for acquittal. In reality they are in periods of respite, and then they are taken suddenly.

**And nothing is lost in the meantime.** The ayah ends with the assurance that "Our messengers record all of that which you plot." Ibn Kathir identifies these as the noble writers — the angels who write the deeds. They write everything that people do and keep count of it, and then present it before the All-Knowing of the seen and unseen worlds. The recompense covers the significant deeds and even the seemingly insignificant, down to something as tiny as a spot on a date pit. A plan hatched in private is still a plan on file.

## Ayah 22: the ship

Now the general truth becomes a scene. Allah says, "He it is Who enables you to travel through land and sea." Ibn Kathir notes that this travelling is itself an act of care: it means that He preserves you and maintains you with His care and His watching. The ordinary journey that ends safely was never self-explanatory.

Then: "till when you are in the ships, and they sail with them with a favorable wind, and they are glad therein." Ibn Kathir's gloss on that sailing is two words: smoothly and calmly. This is the good day, and the verse records only the passengers' gladness — a fair wind, a moving deck, people pleased with their passage.

Then the sentence turns. "Then comes a stormy wind, and the waves come to them **from all sides**." The wind they had been rejoicing in was *rīḥ ṭayyibah*, a favourable wind; what now comes upon the ships is *rīḥ ʿāṣif*, a storm wind. And the waves are not in front of them or behind them; there is no direction that is safe. So, in Ibn Kathir's explanation of "they think that they are encircled," they conclude the obvious: they are going to be destroyed.

### The purest prayer a person ever makes

"Then they invoke Allah, making their faith pure for Him alone." Ibn Kathir's comment on this is the heart of the passage: **in that situation they would not invoke an idol or a statue besides Allah.** They would single Him out alone for their supplications and prayers.

This is worth sitting with. Worship of Allah alone, with nothing beside Him — that is exactly what surfaces on the sinking ship, not as a doctrine argued into someone, but as what is left when terror has stripped away everything false. The idols are not debated; they simply vanish from the mind, because at that moment everyone on board knows who actually holds the sea. Ibn Kathir cites the parallel elsewhere in the Qur'an: "And when harm touches you upon the sea, those that you call upon vanish from you except Him alone. But when He brings you safe to land, you turn away. And man is ever ungrateful" (17:67).

And they make a vow: "If You deliver us from this, we shall truly be of the grateful." Ibn Kathir explains what that promise means in their mouths: *we will not ascribe others as partners with You; we will later worship You alone as we are praying to You here and now.* Gratitude here is not a passing feeling of thanks — it is a commitment to a way of worship. That is the pledge the next ayah measures them against.

## Ayah 23: back on land, as if nothing had happened

"But when He delivers them, behold! They rebel in the earth wrongfully." Ibn Kathir's summary is devastating in its plainness: **they returned as if they had never experienced any difficulties and had never promised Him anything.** He connects it to the earlier verse of this surah: "He passes on as if he had never invoked Us for a harm that touched him" (10:12).

The word for what they do is *baghy* — rendered in these commentaries as rebellion, transgression, disobedience to Allah, and oppression of others — and they do it *bi-ghayri'l-ḥaqq*, wrongfully, with no right on their side at all. The distance between the vow on the deck and the wrongdoing on the shore is the whole subject of the ayah.

### "Your rebellion is only against yourselves"

Then the address widens to the whole of humanity: "O mankind! Your rebellion is only against yourselves." Ibn Kathir: it is you yourselves that will taste the evil consequence of this transgression; you will not harm anyone else with it.

This is the passage's moral centre, and both commentaries press it hard.

Ibn Kathir supports it with a hadith — he cites it without naming a collection, so it is given here as a teaching of the Prophet ﷺ without attribution to any named book: that there is no sin more worthy that Allah hasten its punishment for in this world — on top of the punishment Allah has in store for it in the Hereafter — than oppression and cutting the ties of the womb.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** draws the same conclusion from the wording: the warning "your rebellion is, in fact, against your own selves" tells us that the curse of injustice is certain, and that much before matters are settled in the Hereafter, one guilty of injustice must suffer its evil consequences in this world as well.

Maʿārif then cites two narrations:

- The Prophet ﷺ said that Allah hastens to repay mercy shown to relatives and favour done to people — whereby its blessings start becoming visible in this world, much before the Hereafter — and He also hastens to repay injustices done and relationships severed, in that their consequences have to be faced within the life of this world. *(Reported by Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah with a hasan chain of narrators.)*
- In another hadith narrated by Sayyidah ʿĀ'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), the Prophet ﷺ said there are three sins the curse whereof falls on the sinner himself: injustice, breach of trust, and deception. *(Reported by Abu ash-Shaykh and Ibn Marduwayh in Tafsir) (See Mazhari.)*

Put these beside the ayah and the logic is complete. The man who is delivered from the sea and then wrongs people imagines he has escaped twice — once from drowning, once from his promise. He has escaped nothing. The harm has simply been redirected, and its address is his own soul.

## The last three phrases

The ayah closes by putting the whole transaction in perspective, and each phrase does a job.

**"A brief enjoyment of this worldly life."** Ibn Kathir: you only have a short enjoyment in this low and abased worldly life. Whatever the transgressor gained by his overreach — that is the entire payout. It is not withheld; it is just very small and very brief.

**"Then unto Us is your return."** Ibn Kathir: your goal and final destination. The ship reaches a shore either way.

**"And We shall inform you of what you used to do."** Allah will inform them of all their deeds, and then recompense them for them. Ibn Kathir ends with a line worth memorising: *so let him who finds good in his record praise Allah, and let him who finds other than that blame no one but himself.* That is the same truth as "your rebellion is only against yourselves," now spoken from the far side of the resurrection.

## Living this passage

The passage is not describing an exotic sinner. It is describing a very common person, and the sources make the applications concrete:

- **Say where the blessing came from.** The hadith recorded by Al-Bukhari makes the whole difference hang on one sentence spoken after the rain. Naming Allah as the giver is not a formality; it is the difference that narration draws between belief and disbelief.
- **Keep the promises you made in the storm.** Ibn Kathir defines the vow "we shall be of the grateful" as a pledge to worship Allah alone afterwards as sincerely as you called on Him during the crisis. The test of a desperate duʿā' (supplication) is what your worship looks like once it has been answered.
- **Do not read delay as safety.** Ibn Kathir's explanation of "Allah is more swift in planning" is aimed precisely at the person who concludes from an untroubled life that nothing is being recorded. The respite is real; so are the noble writers, down to the smallest deed.
- **Guard against *baghy*, and cut family ties at your peril.** These two are singled out in the narrations cited by both commentaries as sins whose consequences are hastened into this life, with the Hereafter still to come.
- **Read your own hardships this way.** In this passage the high point of these people's lives is not the calm sailing but the moment of terror, when their faith was pure for Allah alone. If Allah has brought you through something, the ayah is asking you to keep being the person you were when you were calling on Him.

passages.title: Worldly life like rain; the two recompenses
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat set two homes side by side and ask which one you are actually working for. Ayah 24 paints this world as a single season of rain — green, glorious, and gone overnight. Ayah 25 answers it with Allah's own invitation to a home that never ends. Ayat 26 and 27 show the two kinds of people arriving at their two destinations. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces exactly this movement: ayat 24 and 25 compare the two abodes and the states in which their dwellers were, and the verses that follow describe the reward and the punishment of both.

## What comes just before

In ayah 23 Allah warned: *"your rebellion is, in fact, against your own selves."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the point: the curse of injustice is certain, and much before matters are settled in the Hereafter, one who does injustice must suffer its evil consequences in this world as well. It cites the Prophet ﷺ, that Allah hastens to repay mercy shown to relatives and favour done to people, so that its blessings become visible in this world long before the Hereafter — and that He likewise hastens to repay injustices done and relationships severed, so that the consequences have to be faced within the life of this world (reported by Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah with a hasan chain of narrators). It also cites, on the authority of ʿĀʾishah, that there are three sins the curse whereof falls on the sinner himself: injustice, breach of trust, and deception (reported by Abu ash-Shaykh and Ibn Marduwayh in Tafsir; see Mazhari).

## The parable: one season of rain (ayah 24)

*"Verily, the parable of the life of the world is as the water which We send down from the sky; so by it arises the intermingled produce of the earth of which men and cattle eat: until when the earth is clad in its adornments and is beautified, and its people think that they have all the powers of disposal over it, Our command reaches it by night or by day and We make it like a clean-mown harvest, as if it had not flourished yesterday!"*

Ibn Kathir explains that Allah has set an example of the similitude of the life of this world, **its glitter and the swiftness of its passage**, likening it to the plant and vegetation He brings out of the earth by water that comes down from the sky — some of it food for people, such as fruits, and some of it food for cattle, clover plants and herbage. Nothing in the picture is condemned: the rain is a gift, the growth is real, the food is genuinely eaten. The Qur'an is not calling the world evil; it is telling you what kind of thing it is.

**"Clad in its adornments" (أَخَذَتِ الْأَرْضُ زُخْرُفَهَا).** Ibn Kathir pairs this with **وَازَّيَّنَتْ** ("and is beautified"), which he says means the earth became good by what grows on its hills, such as blooming flowers of different shapes and colours. This is the world at its most persuasive: the moment just before harvest, when everything you planted has come good.

**"And its people think that they have all the powers of disposal over it."** Ibn Kathir identifies these people precisely: *those who planted it and put it in the ground* — and their thought is that they are now able to cultivate it and harvest it. The illusion is not wealth; the illusion is **control**. They were right that the crop was ripe. They were wrong that it was theirs to command.

**"Our command reaches it by night or by day."** Ibn Kathir: while they were in that frame of mind, a thunderbolt or a severe, cold storm came to it — it dried its leaves and spoiled its fruits. *Laylan aw nahāran* — by night or by day: there is no safe hour, and whatever schedule you had for it, the command does not consult it.

**"And We make it like a clean-mown harvest" (حَصِيدًا)** — Ibn Kathir: it became dry after it was green and flourishing.

**"As if it had not flourished yesterday" (كَأَن لَّمْ تَغْنَ بِالْأَمْسِ).** Ibn Kathir glosses it: as if nothing existed there before. Qatadah said: "As if it had not flourished; as if it was never blessed." And Ibn Kathir generalises the principle — such are things after they perish, they are as if they had never existed. He points to what Allah said about those who were destroyed: *"So they lay dead, prostrate in their homes; as if they had never lived there"* (11:67–68).

He then cites a hadith that carries the same truth into the next life: a person who led the most prosperous life in this world will be brought up and dipped once in the Fire, and then asked, "Have you ever found any good or comfort?" — and he will reply, "No." And a person who had experienced extreme adversity in this world will be brought up and dipped once in the bliss of Paradise, and then asked, "Did you ever face any hardship or misery?" — and he will reply, "No." One dip erases a lifetime in either direction.

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah gives this same likeness in several ayat of His Noble Book — in Sūrat al-Kahf, *"it is like the water which We send down from the sky, and the vegetation of the earth mingles with it, and becomes fresh and green. But later it becomes dry and broken pieces, which the winds scatter. And Allah is able to do everything"* (18:45) — and similarly in Sūrat az-Zumar (39:21) and Sūrat al-Ḥadīd (57:20).

**"Thus do We explain the Ayat in detail for the people who reflect."** Ibn Kathir: the proofs and evidences are explained in detail so people may take a lesson from this example — the swift vanishing of this world from its people while they are deceived by it. They would trust this world and its promises, and then it unexpectedly turns away from them. And he adds a line worth memorising: **this world, in its nature, runs away from those who seek it, but seeks those who run away from it.**

The parable is aimed at a faculty — *yatafakkarūn*, those who **reflect**. Nothing in ayah 24 is hidden; everyone has watched a season end.

## The invitation: the Abode of Peace (ayah 25)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the sequence closely: in ayah 24, because of the growers' acts of disobedience, some unforeseen Divine punishment descended during the night or the day, and everything stood wiped off as if nothing had existed there. After that comes a description of the life-to-come.

Having mentioned the swiftness of this world and its termination, Ibn Kathir says, Allah invited people to Paradise and encouraged them to seek it — and He called it **Dār as-Salām, the Abode of Peace**, because it is free from defects and miseries.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unfolds the name: a Home where absolute and eternal peace reigns, a Home that has neither pain and sorrow, nor the danger of disease, nor the concern of adverse change or sudden extinction. Every single thing that ruined the crop is absent there. Maʿārif adds a second reason, appearing in some reports from Hadith: Jannah is called the Abode of Peace also because its dwellers shall always be receiving *salām* greetings from Allah and from the angels — indeed the word *salām* would itself be a sort of technical keyword used by the people of Jannah to express their wishes, which the angels would fulfil. ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās said that Dār as-Salām is one of the seven names of Jannah (Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī).

**A practical ruling.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a small but concrete consequence: it is not proper to name a house in this world *Dār as-Salām*, and similarly not correct to give it names like *Jannah* or *Firdaws*.

**Who is being invited.** Ibn Kathir cites the narration of Jābir ibn ʿAbdullāh, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ came out one day and said: "I have seen in my sleep that it was as if Jibrīl was at my head and Mīkāʾīl at my leg. They were saying to each other: 'Give an example for him.' He said: 'Listen, your ear may listen. And fathom, your heart may fathom. The parable of you and your Ummah is that of a king who has built a house on his land. He arranged a banquet in it. Then he sent a messenger to invite the people to his food. Some accepted the invitation and others did not. Allah is the King and the land is Islam, the house is Paradise and you, Muhammad, are the Messenger. Whosoever responds to your call enters Islam. And whosoever enters Islam enters Paradise. And whosoever enters Paradise eats from it.'" Ibn Jarir recorded this hadith.

Ibn Kathir also cites the report from Abū ad-Dardāʾ that the Messenger ﷺ said that two angels descend every day in which the sun rises and say that which all Allah's creatures would hear except jinn and humans: "O people! Come to your Lord! Anything little and sufficient is better than a lot but distractive." And, he says, Allah sent this down in the Qur'an in His words, *"Allah calls to the Abode of Peace."* Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Jarir recorded this.

**Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh's word of advice**, quoted in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, presses the invitation on the individual: "O son of Adam! Allah Almighty invited you to the Home of Peace. When and from which country would you take that right step in response to this Divine call? If you have started making efforts to say yes to this invitation while you are still here in this world, you will succeed — you will reach the Home of Peace. And if you wasted the years of your life here, then landed in your grave, and then thought of following this call, you will be stopped. You will not move from there, not even one step — because the place where you are is no Home of Deeds."

**"And guides whom He wills to a straight path."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān distinguishes two things. The *invitation* to Dār as-Salām is universal — open to all human beings — and in that sense guidance too is open to all. But there is a kind of guidance that is **special**: here a seeker is made to stand on the straight path and given the ability to move ahead on course. This is *tawfīq* at its best, and only fortunate people are blessed with it. So the ayah holds both truths at once: no one is excluded from the call, and no one walks the road except by Allah's granting.

## The two recompenses (ayat 26–27)

**"For those who have done good is the best, and even more"** (ayah 26). Ibn Kathir: those who do good in this world — by having faith and performing righteous deeds — will be rewarded with a good reward in the Hereafter, as Allah says, *"Is there any reward for good other than good?"* (55:60). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies that among those who opted for good, the greatest good was that of *īmān* — belief and faith — supplemented by staunch adherence to righteous deeds; and that such people will have the best of returns, not simply what is coming to them as due, but much more than it.

**What is the "and even more" (وَزِيَادَةٌ)?** Ibn Kathir first lists the obvious increases: the reward on good deeds multiplied ten times to seven hundred times and even more on top of that; what Allah will give them in Paradise, such as the palaces, al-Ḥūr (the virgins of Paradise), and His pleasure upon them; and what He has hidden for them of the delight of the eye. Then he says that on top of all of that, and even better, is the honour of **looking at His Noble Face** — the increase that is greater than anything that had been given.

He names those who explained *ziyādah* this way: Abu Bakr, Ḥudhayfah ibn al-Yamān, ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās, Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyib, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Abī Laylā, ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān ibn Sābiṭ, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, ʿĀmir ibn Saʿd, ʿAṭāʾ, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, as-Suddī, Muhammad ibn Isḥāq, and others from the earlier and later scholars. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Prophet ﷺ himself gave the tafsir of this verse: *al-ḥusnā* here means Jannah, and *ziyādah* means the visit to the most exalted Allah with which the people of Jannah shall be honoured (Tafsīr al-Qurṭubī, on the authority of Anas).

Ibn Kathir cites what Imam Ahmad recorded from Ṣuhayb, that Allah's Messenger ﷺ recited this ayah and then said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, a caller will say: 'O people of Paradise, Allah has promised you something that He wishes to fulfil.' They will reply: 'What is it? Has He not made our Scale heavy? Has He not made our faces white and delivered us from the Fire?' Allah will then remove the veil and they will see Him. By Allah, they have not been given anything dearer to them and more delightful than looking at Him." Muslim and a group of the Imams also related this hadith. In Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's telling of Ṣuhayb's narration, appearing in the Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim, the people of Jannah then discover that this was a blessing far more sublime than all the other blessings of Jannah — something the Lord of all the worlds bestowed upon them without their having to ask for it, simply out of His infinite affection and mercy.

And this greatest of gifts is not earned. Ibn Kathir states it plainly: they will not deserve that because of their deeds — **rather, they will receive it by the grace of Allah and His mercy**.

**The faces (end of ayah 26).** *"Neither darkness nor dust nor any humiliating disgrace shall cover their faces."* Ibn Kathir: no blackness or darkness will be on their faces during the different events of the Day of Judgement — whereas the faces of the rebellious disbelievers will be stained with dust and darkness. Nor will the believers be humiliated, internally or externally; on the contrary, they will be protected and honoured, as Allah has said, *"So Allah saved them from the evil of that Day, and gave them brightness and joy"* (76:11) — meaning, Ibn Kathir explains, light in their faces and delight in their hearts. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that their faces will remain free of any effects of distaste, pain or sorrow, nor will they have to worry about any disgrace — precisely the conditions everyone faces in this mortal world at one time or another, and which those who go to Jahannam will face in the Hereafter.

**"As for those who have earned evil deeds, the recompense of an evil deed is the like thereof"** (ayah 27). Ibn Kathir marks the contrast sharply: after telling us about the state of those happy people who have done right and *promising them increase in reward*, Allah tells us about the unlucky, miserable ones — and here He tells us of **His justice** with them: He will reward them with similar evil, **without any increase**. The asymmetry is the message: the good deed is answered with *al-ḥusnā wa ziyādah*, the evil deed with an exact equivalent and no more. Mercy exceeds; justice matches.

The rest of ayah 27 stacks up what the wrongdoers will have. Their faces will be covered and overtaken by humiliation, Ibn Kathir says, because of their sins and their fear from these sins — as in *"And you will see them brought forward to it, made humble by disgrace"* (42:45), and as in *"Consider not that Allah is unaware of that which the wrongdoers do, but He gives them respite up to a Day when the eyes will stare in horror"* (14:42–43). **"No defender will they have from Allah"** — meaning there will be no protectors to prevent them from punishment, as in *"On that Day man will say: Where is the refuge to flee? No! There is no refuge! Unto your Lord alone will be the place of rest that Day"* (75:10–12). And **"their faces covered as it were with pieces from the darkness of night"** means their faces will be dark in the Hereafter, as in *"On the Day when some faces will become white and some faces will become black"* (3:106–107) and *"Some faces that Day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing; and other faces that Day will be dust-stained"* (80:38–40). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pictures it as darkness so deep it is as if layers upon layers of a night had covered them up.

## Living it

The passage does not ask you to stop planting the field. It asks you to stop believing you own it.

- **Enjoy the world without trusting it.** Ibn Kathir's warning is against *trusting* this world and its promises, because that is precisely when it unexpectedly turns away. The crop was real; the sense of command over it was the mistake.
- **Answer the invitation now.** Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh's point is that the response has to be made here, because the grave is no Home of Deeds. The banquet in the Prophet's ﷺ dream is already prepared; the only variable is whether a person accepts the invitation.
- **Prefer little and sufficient.** The angels' daily call — "anything little and sufficient is better than a lot but distractive" — is a usable test for any increase in income or commitments: not only "is it lawful?" but "does it distract?"
- **Aim above the palaces.** The greatest thing given in Jannah is not its gardens but the sight of its Lord, and Ibn Kathir says it comes not by deeds but by Allah's grace and mercy. That should reorder what a believer asks for in duʿāʾ.
- **Take the asymmetry as encouragement.** Your good is answered with more than its due; your evil, only with its like. That is the shape of dealing with the Most Merciful, and it makes turning back to Him worth attempting rather than futile.

passages.title: The Day partners disown their worshippers
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is.** In three ayat the curtain lifts on one scene of the Day of Resurrection: Allah gathers all of creation, orders those who worshipped others alongside Him to halt in place together with the "partners" they worshipped, cuts the bond between them — and then the partners disown, to their faces, the people who gave them their devotion. What holds the three together is a single movement: from the gathering, to the confrontation, to the collapse. Ayah 28 sets the scene and gives the command; ayah 29 records what the partners say in their defence; ayah 30 shows what is left standing when the whole structure falls away — each soul alone with what it sent forth, returned to Allah, its one real Master.

## Ayah 28: everyone, and no one left behind

The passage opens by asking us to consider "the Day We will gather them all together." Ibn Kathir stresses the scope of that gathering: Allah will gather together all the creatures of the earth, human and jinn, the righteous and the rebellious alike. He reads it alongside another ayah, "and We shall gather them all together so as to leave not one of them behind" (18:47). Nobody slips away. Not one is left behind.

Then comes the command: **"Stop at your place! You and your partners."** Ibn Kathir explains that Allah will then command the idolaters to stay where they are and not to move from their destined places, so that they are separated from the place of the believers. He gathers the other passages where the Qur'an describes exactly this sorting: "And O you the criminals! Get you apart this Day (from the believers)" (36:59); "And on the Day when the Hour will be established — that Day shall (all men) be separated" (30:14); and, from the same surah, "On that Day men shall be divided" (30:43), which he glosses as: they shall be divided in two.

That is the first thing this Day does — it un-mixes. In this world believer and idolater live side by side, indistinguishable in the crowd. There, the crowd is sorted into two, and each person's true company becomes visible.

Ibn Kathir places this scene at what will take place when Allah Almighty comes for the Final Judgement, and mentions that the believers intercede to Allah so that the Final Judgement may come and they be rid of that state. He cites the Prophet ﷺ saying that on the Day of Resurrection "we will be in a visible place above the [other] people." (The source quotes these words without naming the collection they come from, so we pass on the teaching without attaching it to a named book.)

## The bond is cut: "Then We shall separate them"

The idolater and his object of worship stood shoulder to shoulder in the world — the idols, and the satans who had led them astray. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the point plainly: after this, the connection between these people and their so-called gods, as it existed in the mortal world, will be disconnected. It also notes that the ones being addressed here are not only carved stones; the dialogue is between the people of Jahannam and "the idols or satans who had led them astray."

And notice the reason Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives for the summons itself: they are told to stay in their places with their gods "so that you can find out the reality of your conviction." This is not a trial in which the verdict is uncertain. It is an exposure. The idolater is made to stand next to the very thing he built his life around and watch what it does when it matters.

What it does is turn on him. **"It was not us that you used to worship."** Ibn Kathir brings the parallel verses so we hear how consistently the Qur'an says this: "Nay, but they will deny their worship of them" (19:82); "When those who were followed declare themselves innocent of those who followed (them)" (2:166); and the sharpest of them, "And who is more astray than one who calls on, besides Allah, such as will not answer him till the Day of Resurrection, and who are (even) unaware of their calls to them? And when mankind are gathered, they (false deities) will become their enemies" (46:5–6). Ibn Kathir points out that in our passage this refers to the partners responding to those who worshipped them — the one and only reply they ever give, and it is a repudiation.

Read those verses together and the tragedy is complete. In this life the false god does not answer, and is unaware of the calls made to it. On that Day it finally speaks — and its first words are a denial, its posture that of an enemy. Every prayer poured into it for a lifetime is revealed to have gone nowhere at all.

## Ayah 29: "So sufficient is Allah as a witness between us and you"

The disowning is put under oath, and the irony is severe: the very Being these people set partners beside is now called upon by those partners as the Witness who can settle the matter.

Ibn Kathir unpacks their plea. They say that they did not know or think that these people were worshipping them; then, with Allah as Witness between them, come three denials — we never called upon you to worship us, we never ordered you to worship us, and neither did we accept your worship of us. Whatever the worshipper felt was flowing between him and the object of his devotion was flowing in one direction only, and it was never received.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān supplies the blunt reason for the idols' claim of ignorance: they had "no senses, no movement and no intelligence to understand these matters." The thing a man knelt to, wept before, arranged his year around, could not so much as register that he was there.

## Ayah 30: alone with what you sent forth

**"There! Every person will know (exactly) what he had earned before."** The ayah begins by fixing a place — *there*, at that spot. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names it: the plain of Resurrection, which it calls an excruciating place. The passage has been describing a crowd; now the attention turns to the individual.

The sources render this reckoning in two complementary directions — knowing, and facing the consequences. Ibn Kathir explains it as the state of accounting on the Day of Resurrection: every soul shall know all that it had sent forth, both good and evil. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says that in that place everyone would have assessed his or her respective deeds, individually and personally, whether they were beneficial or harmful. On that plain, seeing the truth of what you did and receiving its consequence are one and the same event.

And what is assessed is what was *sent forth*. Nothing arrives in the next life except what was despatched from this one. Ibn Kathir lines up the verses that describe this reckoning: "The Day when all the secrets will be examined" (86:9); "On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward, and what he left behind" (75:13); and "…and on the Day of Resurrection, We shall bring out for him a book which he will find wide open. (It will be said to him): 'Read your book. You yourself are sufficient as a reckoner against you this Day'" (17:13–14).

Notice what has happened across the passage. In ayah 29 the partners said *sufficient is Allah as a witness*; in 17:14 the man is told *you yourself are sufficient as a reckoner*. Every prop has been removed. The partner he relied on has disowned him, and his own book is opened in front of him.

## "Returned to Allah, their rightful Mawlā"

"And they will be brought back to Allah, their rightful *Mawlā*." Ibn Kathir's rendering keeps the Arabic word and glosses it simply as *Lord*. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the same return: they will all be taken to their true Lord, the only One worthy of worship.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws the line under everything else: at that time, all options of trust and support one usually looks up to will stand terminated — and even the idols the Mushriks used to take as their patrons and intercessors will evaporate in thin air, the whole lot of them at once.

Ibn Kathir explains the return in terms of authority: all affairs and matters will be brought back to Allah, the Judge, the All-Just; He will judge everyone, and then admit the people of Paradise into Paradise and the people of Hell to Hell.

That single word *al-ḥaqq* — rendered "rightful" by Ibn Kathir and "true" by Maʿārif ul Qurʼān — is the verdict on everything the passage has shown. There was only ever one genuine Master. The others were positions people appointed, not realities.

**"And their invented false deities will vanish from them."** Ibn Kathir's gloss is exact and unsentimental: what vanishes is what the idolaters worshipped, and what they worshipped besides Allah was something *they invented*. It disappears on that Day because there was never anything solid there to begin with — the losing of it is simply the truth becoming visible.

## Living it

The passage is aimed at open idolatry, and it should not be stretched past what it says. But its logic reaches every heart.

- **Test your attachments by that scene.** Stand each thing you rely on in the position this passage puts them in: on the plain of Resurrection, does it speak for you, or does it say "you never worshipped us"? Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's phrase is worth keeping — every option of trust and support one usually looks up to stands terminated there. Only what was directed to Allah survives the sorting.
- **Conviction is not the same as truth.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives the reason they are made to stand beside their gods: "so that you can find out the reality of your conviction." The conviction was real. Its object was not — and had, in its own words, no senses and no awareness of them at all.
- **Send it ahead.** What each soul meets is what it sent forth. Whatever is not despatched from this life will not be found waiting in the next.
- **Take Allah as your *Mawlā* now.** The return to Allah in ayah 30 is not optional; they are all brought back. The only question is whether He was your acknowledged Lord before you were returned to Him, or only after every substitute had vanished.

passages.title: "Who provides for you?" — that is Allah
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat are a single argument, and it is one of the most disarming arguments in the Qur'an. The Prophet ﷺ is told to put a short series of questions to the idolators — questions to which they already know the answer. Ayah 31 asks them and reports the answer they cannot avoid giving: "Allah." Ayah 32 draws the conclusion that answer forces. Ayah 33 states what happens to a person who hears the conclusion and still refuses it.

What holds the passage together is that the evidence is *theirs*. Nothing new is revealed to them here. Their own admission is picked up and turned into the case against them.

## The one move the passage makes

Ibn Kathir heads this section: "The Idolators recognize Allah's Tawhid in Lordship and the Evidence is established against Them through this Recognition." He explains that "Allah argues that the idolators' recognition of Allah's Oneness in Lordship is an evidence against them, for which they should admit and recognize the Oneness in divinity and worship."

Two things are being distinguished, and the whole passage turns on the distance between them:

- **Oneness in Lordship** — that Allah alone creates, provides, gives life, and runs the universe.
- **Oneness in divinity and worship** — that Allah alone is therefore to be worshipped and obeyed.

They granted the first. What they would not do was let it govern the second. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the challenge in exactly those terms: "When you know that it is Allah alone who creates, sustains and manages everything, why do you have to take someone else other than Him as deserving of your devotion and obedience?" You have already granted the premise; the conclusion is not optional.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān also notes the tone of it. In ayat 31 and 32, it says, the Qur'an "has, in its typically wise and patronizing manner, beamed a few questions at the Mushriks to help them regain their sanity." Not abuse, not a lecture — questions. And the Prophet ﷺ is instructed only to *ask* them: **qul**, "Say," is the first word of ayah 31.

## Ayah 31, question one: who provides for you from the sky and the earth?

Ibn Kathir explains this as: "who is He Who sends down water from the sky and splits the earth with His power and will and allows things to grow from it." He connects it to Allah's words elsewhere: "Is there a god, besides Allah?" (27:62), and the list of what that provision actually looks like — "Grains. And grapes and clover plants. And olives and date palms. And gardens dense with many trees. And fruits and herbage" (80:27–31).

Notice the two directions the question sweeps: **from the sky** (the water that comes down) **and the earth** (what pushes up through the split soil). Between those two lies the whole of what feeds you — the grain, the grapes, the olives, the dates, the dense gardens, the fruit.

Ibn Kathir then presses the point with a further ayah: "Who is he that can provide for you if He should withhold His provision?" (67:21). Provision is not a standing fact of nature that simply continues on its own. It is a continuous act of giving. If the giving stopped, no one is standing by to take over the supply.

## Question two: who owns hearing and sight?

The Arabic is *amman yamliku al-samʿa wal-abṣār* — literally, who **owns** hearing and sight. Not who made them once; who holds them now.

Ibn Kathir: "Allah is the One who granted you the power of sight and hearing. If He willed otherwise, He would remove these gifts and deprive you of them." He cites two ayat as parallels: "Say it is He Who has created you, and endowed you with hearing and seeing" (67:23), and "Say: 'Tell me, if Allah took away your hearing and your sight'" (6:46).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts it as sharply as it can be put: He is "the master-controller of your ears and eyes in that you hear and see as He wills and you do not if He wills otherwise."

This is the question that reaches inside a person's own body. Provision comes from outside you and can feel like the world's routine; your eyes and ears are *you*. And even they are held on loan.

## Question three: who brings the living from the dead, and the dead from the living?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks both halves with entirely ordinary examples:

- The living from the dead: "vegetation and trees from the soil," and "humans and animals from the sperm, or a bird from an egg."
- The dead from the living: "a lifeless sperm from humans and animals."

Ibn Kathir's comment on the whole clause is short and worth keeping: this happens "by His great power and grace." Not power alone — power *and* grace. The machinery of life turning over is a kindness, not merely a display of force.

Nothing in these examples is exotic. The argument is deliberately built out of soil, seed, egg and birth: the things that are so ordinary they stop registering as evidence.

## Question four: who manages the affair?

*Wa man yudabbir al-amr* — who plans, arranges, disposes, manages. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it: "who is it that plans and manages the affairs of the whole universe?"

Ibn Kathir answers with a run of questions of his own, and it is the densest passage in his commentary here:

> "In Whose Hand is the dominion of everything? Who protects all, while against Whom there is no protector? Who is the One who judges with none reversing His judgement? Who is the One that is not questioned about what He does while they will be questioned?"

Take that third and fourth line seriously. Every human authority can be appealed over the head of; every human authority can be called to account. Here is One whose judgement has no court above it and who answers to no one — while every one of us will answer.

He then quotes: "Whosoever is in the heavens and on earth begs of Him. Every day He is (engaged) in some affair!" (55:29), and comments: "The upper and lower kingdoms and what is in them both, including the angels, humans, and Jinn are in desperate need of Him. They are His servants and are under His control."

Note what that sweeps in. Not only humans and jinn but the angels too are counted among those in desperate need, His servants and under His control. There is no rank of creation high enough to step out of the queue of beggars — so there is no rank of creation worth worshipping.

## The answer, and the sting

The Qur'an does not wait for the reply. It supplies it: *fa-sayaqūlūna Allāh* — "**They will say: 'Allah.'**" The answer is announced before the question has even been put, because there is no other answer available to them.

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line, and it is the hinge of the whole passage: "they say this knowingly and they admit it." This is not a slip or a concession dragged out of them. They know it.

So: *fa-qul afalā tattaqūn* — "Say: 'Will you not then be afraid?'" Ibn Kathir glosses: "don't you fear Him when you worship others because of your ignorance and false opinions?" The fear being asked for here is not a vague spirituality; it is what a person ought to feel when he knows exactly who runs everything and directs his devotion elsewhere anyway.

## Ayah 32: "That, then, is Allah, your Lord in truth"

*Fa-dhālikumu-llāhu rabbukumu-l-ḥaqq.* The demonstrative "that" reaches back and gathers up everything they just conceded — the water and the crops, the eyes, the ears, the living and the dead, the running of the universe — and says: that is who Allah is. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "this is the Sacred Being whose attributes of perfection have just been mentioned."

And now the conclusion they have been avoiding. Ibn Kathir: "This Lord that you admitted is the One Who does all this, is your Lord and the True Deity that deserves to be worshipped alone."

**"So after the truth, what else can there be, save error?"** Ibn Kathir: "any one worshipped other than Him is false, for there is none worthy of worship but Allah, He Has no partners." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "Once you have found the Truth, there remains nothing else to find except error and straying… once it stands proved that Allah Taʿālā is the only true and rightful object of worship, it is terribly senseless to abandon this truth and allow yourself to be diverted elsewhere."

**"How then are you turned away?"** — *fa-annā tuṣrafūn*. Even the English rendering keeps the passive: you are being *turned*, diverted, steered off. Ibn Kathir: "How then can you turn away from His worship to worship others while you know that He is the Lord that has created everything, the One who controls and governs everything?"

The question is not "why do you not know?" It is "how, knowing this, do you still get pulled away?" That is a question about the heart, not the intellect.

### A point of creed drawn from this ayah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān flags an important principle here. The words "What is there, after truth, but error?" prove that **there is no middle ground between truth and error** in matters of belief. Whatever is not the truth falls under error and straying; there is no third category that is neither; and two opposite positions cannot both be the truth. This, it says, "is an established rule in the sight of the majority of scholars in the Muslim Ummah."

It then adds a qualification that matters enormously in practice, and it is careful to attribute the views rather than flatten them. In **minor and subsidiary juristic issues** — questions of law settled by *ijtihād*, the qualified scholar's reasoned effort to derive a ruling — the scholars differ. In the view of some of them, both sides would be considered as on truth in ijtihād-based issues. And "according to the majority of them, there is consensus on the view that the taking of contra-position in Ijtihad-based problems cannot be termed as error and straying."

So the hard line of ayah 32 is drawn where the ayah itself draws it: around *who is worshipped*. It is not a licence to brand every fellow Muslim who follows a different position on a point of law as "misguided."

## Ayah 33: the Word proven true

*Kadhālika ḥaqqat kalimatu rabbika ʿalā-lladhīna fasaqū* — "Thus is the Word of your Lord justified against those who rebel, that they will not believe."

*Kadhālika*, "thus" or "in this way," ties the verdict to what just happened. The sentence is not arbitrary; it follows the refusal.

Ibn Kathir traces the whole chain: "These idolators disbelieved and continued to practice their Shirk, and worship others beside Allah. But they knew that He is the Creator, the Sustainer and the only One of authority and control in this universe, the One Who sent His Messengers to single Him out for all worship. As they disbelieved and were persistent in their Shirk, Allah's Word proved true and was justified that they would be miserable inhabitants of the Fire."

Every element of the condemnation was supplied by them: they knew, they were told, they persisted. Ibn Kathir closes with the scene where this is admitted out loud: "They will say: 'Yes,' but the Word of torment has been justified against the disbelievers!" (39:71).

Note also who the ayah names: *alladhīna fasaqū*, those who **rebelled** — Ibn Kathir's text glosses it "disobey Allah." The charge is not ignorance. It is stepping outside obedience with your eyes open. That is precisely what the four questions of ayah 31 were designed to establish.

## Living it

**Answer the questions yourself.** The passage is built as an interrogation, and its power is lost if you only watch someone else being asked. Where did today's food come from — trace it back past the shop, past the field, to the water sent down and the split soil. Whose is the hearing you are using to read this?

**Watch for the gap.** The problem the passage exposes was not what they believed about Allah; it was the distance between what they *admitted* and whom they actually turned to and obeyed. A believer can carry the same gap in a different shape: saying with full conviction that Allah alone provides, while the actual fear in the chest is of the employer, the market, or the family's disapproval. Ayah 32's question is the diagnostic one — *how are you turned away?*

**Nothing is on autopilot.** "Every day He is (engaged) in some affair" (55:29), and everything in the heavens and the earth is begging of Him. Provision is a continuing act, sight is held, the affair of the universe is being managed right now. That is either a terrifying thought or a restful one, depending entirely on whether you have settled the question of ayah 32.

**Argue the way the passage argues.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's description of the method is worth imitating: wise, kindly questions, aimed at helping someone "regain their sanity." Ibn Kathir's whole case rests on what the other side already accepts. When you speak to someone about Allah, the strongest ground is not what they deny — it is what they have already granted.

passages.title: Can your gods create or guide? Only conjecture
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat form one cross-examination, and they are best read as a single movement rather than three separate verses. Allah instructs His Prophet ﷺ to put two questions to those who worship others alongside Him — *can any of your partners originate the creation and then repeat it? can any of them guide to the truth?* — and in each case He supplies the answer Himself before the opponents can stall. Then ayah 36 names what had actually been carrying them along: not evidence, but conjecture. Ibn Kathir sums up the whole passage in a sentence: this "invalidates and falsifies their claims for committing Shirk with Allah and worshipping different idols and rivals." (*Shirk* is associating partners with Allah in what belongs to Him alone.)

One line of reasoning runs through all three ayat. Worship belongs to the One who originates the creation and repeats it, and who alone turns hearts from the wrong path to the right path. Whatever can do neither has no claim on you — and, as ayah 36 explains, whoever follows it anyway is following an assumption rather than a proof.

## Where the argument starts: after truth, only error

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān anchors this passage in what came just before, in ayah 32: *"So, that is Allah, your Lord in truth. And what is there, after truth, but error?"* That, it says, is "the Sacred Being whose attributes of perfection have just been mentioned. Once you have found the Truth, there remains nothing else to find except error and straying." Once it stands proved that Allah alone is the true and rightful object of worship, "it is terribly senseless to abandon this truth and allow yourself to be diverted elsewhere."

Ayat 34–36 are the follow-through on that sentence. If there is no third place to stand between truth and error, then the only honest question left is whether what you worship can actually do anything.

## The first question: who originates the creation and repeats it?

**"Say: 'Is there of your partners one that originates the creation and then repeats it?'"**

The Arabic pairs two verbs: *yabda'u al-khalq* — "originates the creation" — and *thumma yuʿīduhu* — "then repeats it."

Ibn Kathir unpacks the question by widening it until it can only have one answer: "who is the one who started the creation of these heavens and earth and created all the creatures in them? Who can place the planets and the stars in their positions? Who can then repeat the process of the creation?" Notice what is being asked for. Not what the partner-gods can argue, but who can *do* these things — start, place, repeat.

Then the answer, given to the Prophet ﷺ to pronounce: **"Say: 'Allah.'"** Ibn Kathir's gloss is short and complete: "It is He Who does this. He does it by Himself, alone without partners." Originating and repeating creation is not shared work. There is no assistant in it.

**"Then how are you deluded away (from the truth)?"** — *fa-annā tu'fakūn.* Ibn Kathir: "How is it that you are so misled from the right path to falsehood?" The question is put as a rebuke rather than a request for information: having admitted where creation comes from, what could possibly have turned you the other way?

## The same question turned inward: who guides to the truth?

The second question has exactly the same shape as the first, which is why the two belong together. But where the first pointed outward — heavens, earth, planets, stars — this one points inward.

**"Say: 'Is there of your partners one that guides to the truth?'"**

Ibn Kathir puts it plainly: "You know that your deities are incapable of guiding those who are astray. It is Allah alone Who guides the misled and confused ones and turns the hearts from the wrong path to the right path. It is Allah, none has the right to be worshipped but He."

Follow the order of those sentences. Ibn Kathir moves directly from the fact that Allah alone turns hearts to the conclusion that He alone has the right to be worshipped. That is the same move ayah 34 made with creation, now made with guidance — and it is why the two questions are asked side by side.

Again the answer is supplied before the opponents can stall: **"Say: 'It is Allah who guides to the truth...'"**

## What both questions add up to: the comparison

Having established who creates and who guides, the ayah puts the choice as a comparison: *"Is then He Who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who finds not guidance (himself) unless he is guided?"*

The two sides are deliberately lopsided. On one side, the One who guides *to* the truth. On the other, one who cannot find guidance for himself unless someone else guides him. The question answers itself, which is exactly why it is asked as a question.

Ibn Kathir presses the choice: "Will the servant then follow the one who guides to the truth so that he may see after he was blind, or follow one who doesn't guide to anything except towards blindness and muteness?" Following the One who guides ends in sight. Following what cannot guide ends in "blindness and muteness."

**Ibrahim's argument, quoted by Ibn Kathir.** To show this is not a new line of reasoning, Ibn Kathir brings the words of Ibrahim (peace be upon him) to his father: *"O my father! Why do you worship that which hears not, sees not and cannot avail you in anything?"* (19:42) — and to his people: *"Worship you that which you (yourselves) carve? While Allah has created you and what you make!"* (37:95–96). Ibn Kathir notes that "there are many Ayat in this regard."

That second quotation is worth sitting with. The worshipper carves the object, so the object depends on the worshipper; and, as the ayah says, Allah created both the carver and what he makes. The dependence runs one way only, and worship should run back up it.

**"Then, what is the matter with you? How judge you?"** — *fa-mā lakum kayfa taḥkumūn.* Ibn Kathir reads this as an appeal to their own reason: "What is the matter with you? What has happened to your mind? How did you make Allah's creatures equal to Him? What kind of judgement did you make to turn away from Allah and worship this or that? Why did you not worship the Lord — Glorified be He, the True King, the Judge and the One Who guides to the truth? Why didn't you call upon Him alone and turn towards Him?"

In Ibn Kathir's framing they had, in effect, delivered a verdict — making "Allah's creatures equal to Him" — and the ayah asks them to look at the verdict they delivered.

## Why the two questions went unanswered: conjecture

Ayah 36 supplies the diagnosis, and it is what holds the passage together: **"And most of them follow nothing but conjecture. Certainly, conjecture can be of no avail against the truth."**

Ibn Kathir: "Allah then explained that they did not follow their own religion out of evidence and proof. The fact is that they were following mere conjecture and imagination. But conjecture is in no way a substitute for the truth."

That is the answer to why neither challenge could be met. Their position was never built out of evidence in the first place, so there was never anything to bring to a contest about who creates and who guides.

The Arabic word here is *ẓann*. The translation before us renders it "inherited assumptions"; Ibn Kathir's rendering has "conjecture," and his comment pairs it with "imagination." Between them they describe something absorbed rather than established — and, as Ibn Kathir says, "in no way a substitute for the truth."

Note also that the wording is "most of them," not all of them.

## The closing line: "Allah is All-Aware of what they do"

Ibn Kathir reads this closing line two ways at once: "This is both a threat and a promise of severe punishment. Allah said that He would reward them for their actions with a complete reward."

So the ayah that exposes their conjecture ends by naming the One from whom nothing they do is hidden — and who will recompense them for their actions in full.

## A note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: is there a middle ground?

Because ayah 36 turns on truth versus conjecture, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's discussion of ayah 32 belongs here. From *"What is there, after truth, but error?"* it draws a rule of belief: "there is no intermediary link between truth and error. What is not the truth will be included in error and straying. There can be no such thing that is neither truth nor error. And it is also not possible that two opposite things could be the truth." This, it says, "is an established rule in the sight of the majority of scholars in the Muslim Ummah."

But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān immediately marks the limit of that rule, and the distinction is important. "Difference exists among ʿUlamāʼ regarding minor and subsidiary juristic issues" — that is, detailed questions of law rather than of belief. On such matters, settled by *ijtihād* (a qualified scholar's reasoned effort to derive a ruling where the evidence admits more than one reading), some scholars held that both sides would be considered as on truth; and, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, "according to the majority of them, there is consensus on the view that the taking of contra-position in Ijtihad-based problems cannot be termed as error and straying."

So the severity of these ayat is aimed where it belongs. On the question of who creates and who guides, there is no third position: it is truth or it is error. On the "minor and subsidiary juristic issues" where trained scholars read the evidence differently, the same knife does not cut. Treating a juristic disagreement as though it were the *shirk* of ayah 34 misapplies the passage.

## Living it

**Put the two questions to whatever you rely on.** Ibn Kathir turns the ayat into a test anyone can apply: who started the creation, who placed the planets and the stars in their positions, who can repeat the process of the creation — and who "turns the hearts from the wrong path to the right path"? Whatever can do none of this has no claim to your worship, however much weight you have been placing on it.

**Check whether your religion rests on evidence or on assumption.** Ibn Kathir's charge against them was not that they were unintelligent but that they "did not follow their own religion out of evidence and proof," following instead "mere conjecture and imagination." Ask, of the beliefs you hold most confidently: do I know this, or did I absorb it?

**Ask guidance from the only One who gives it.** Since it is Allah alone who "guides the misled and confused ones and turns the hearts from the wrong path to the right path," guidance is something to be asked for, not assumed. Ibn Kathir's own question is the practical instruction: *"Why didn't you call upon Him alone and turn towards Him?"*

**Follow the One most worthy of being followed.** Ayah 35 does not merely refute the idols; it asks who deserves your allegiance: "He Who guides to the truth," or "he who finds not guidance (himself) unless he is guided." Of anything else competing for your allegiance, ask which of those two positions it is in.

passages.title: The Qur'an could not be forged: the challenge
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is doing**

These four ayat answer one question: where did this Qur'an come from? Ayah 37 states what the Book is. Ayah 38 turns the accusation of forgery into a public test. Ayah 39 says why the deniers refused anyway. Ayah 40 tells the Prophet ﷺ that the people he was sent to will divide over it, and leaves the knowledge of who is who with Allah. Ibn Kathir's heading over the whole block sums up its claim: the Qur'an is "the True, Inimitable Word of Allah and It is a Miracle."

## Ayah 37: what the Qur'an is

Ibn Kathir opens with the claim in its widest form: "The Qur'an has a miraculous nature that cannot be imitated. No one can produce anything similar to the Qur'an, nor ten Surahs or even one Surah like it." The ayah then makes three statements that build on each other.

**First: it could not have been produced by anyone other than Allah.** *Wa mā kāna hādhā'l-Qur'ānu an yuftarā min dūni'llāh* — "And this Qur'an is not such as could ever be produced by other than Allah." Ibn Kathir glosses it plainly: "a book like this cannot be but from Allah. This is not similar to the speech uttered by humans."

Notice what the argument rests on. Ibn Kathir grounds it in two things at once. One is the text itself — "the eloquence, clarity, precision and grace of the Qur'an cannot be but from Allah," together with "the great and abundant principles and meanings within the Qur'an, which are of great benefit in this world and for the Hereafter." The other is a point of creed, stated in his own words: "There is nothing like His High Self and Attributes or like His sayings and actions. Therefore His Words are not like the words of His creatures." If the Speaker is like nothing else, His speech will be like nothing else. That is the logic underneath the ayah, and it is why the impossibility here is not merely "nobody happened to manage it" but that such a book "cannot be but from Allah."

**Second: it confirms what came before.** *Taṣdīq alladhī bayna yadayh* — "a confirmation of the revelation which was before it." Ibn Kathir explains: these are "previous revelations and Books. The Qur'an confirms these books and is a witness to them. It shows the changes, perversions and corruption that have taken place within these Books." A witness both endorses and testifies — the Qur'an affirms what those revelations carried, and standing over them as witness it also exposes what was altered in them.

**Third: it explains in full.** *Tafṣīl al-kitāb* — "a full explanation of the Book." Ibn Kathir glosses it as "fully and truly explaining and detailing the rules and the lawful and the unlawful."
